div.head: MUNICIPAL ELBCTIONS, 1893. TO THE BURGESSES OF Si'. JOUN'S WARD.
div.p: MUNICIPAL ELBCTIONS, 1893. TO THE BURGESSES OF Si'. JOUN'S WARD.
LADIES AND GENTLEMSN,-.

At the desire of your Ward Committee and with the unanimous approval and support of the Conservatives of the Ward, I have much pleasure in offering you ay service, a, a representative of the Ward. It will be my endeavour at all times to see that tie sanitary condition of the ward, includ- ing the paving of streets and back passages and lighting of same, obtains prompt attention. I am in favour of-good wages and fair prices, and I condemn sweating In every shape and form. I shall be ever ready to receive suggestions from any of the burgesses of the ward, and where any grievance or object detrimental to the true interests of the burgesses exists, I shall give Italy most strenuous opposition until it be removed. Should you do me the honour to cleat me. my constant aim in the Town Council will be to do all in my power for the improvement of the town and its trade, so as to create labour and wages for the working classes, and business for the shopkeepers and commercial interest. I therefore with confidence appeal to you for your votes and suppoist on Otte day of election. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, JOHN BAIRD. Labarnum-vilia, Proghall-lane, Warrington, October 12th 1198.

div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY DEAR NELLIE,

Velvet hats always look seasonable as the cold comes on, and they are the only ones now worn without a quantity of feathers, though they are not entirely without. Every feather to be found in a pheasant's plumage is utilised in small made- up ornaments that are not breasts and do not pre- tend to be wings. Rosettes of velvet and chiffon have quite taken the place of bows, and are placed chiefly at the back, the feathers being in front. Tcques, instead of being all round alike, are wide in front, and frequently adorned with gold and twists of two contrasting velvets. The mushroom and sailor shapes are too.abecoming to disappear yet, but they often have soft crowns of microir velvet or fancy velvet sewn with spangles. Hand- some buckles are seen on all hats, but ome is con- sidered enough, whereas a few months ago several small ones were worn at a time.

Smooth felts striped with narrow hairy bands are among the novelties of the moment, but they are not particularly stylish, and do not promise to wear well. Gathered and rucked velvet is again largely used in millinery, and for " dressy " occa- sions nothing can be nicer than a large drooping shape in black gathered velvet with a full, jet.. embroidered crown and a trimming of black ostrich feathers and handsome jet pins. The feathers are nearly always arranged to start from the front, by the way, and are arranged with as little formality as possible. Fashion ordains, however, that they should be long, full, and sweeping, so that their cost is considerable, and, unfortunately, the broad, flat. brimmed, low-crowned type of hat seems to lack style if it is not equipped with these expensive plumes, some of which are rendered even inure costly by having strips of fur—chinchilla, sable or ermine—sewn down the ribs. For the smaller and.more useful class of felt bats, large hunches of fine hackle-feathers are in vogue, and these are occasionally placed at the side, but far oftener rise immediately in front, falling over the crown. Spotted feathers are fashionable, and sequinned and jetted ones are not yet out of favour, despite the suspicion of vulgarity that always accom - panies them.

A tailor-made jacket of black box cloth is fashionable and handsomely braided. The revers are cut in a novel shape, and the high collar can be worn either up or down. A very handsome black coat-tailed jacket suit- able for a tall woman with a good figure, is made of black Velours du Nord, trimmel with Wank fox fur, black passementerie in handsome motifs, that just diversify the front without concealing it, and the whole is lined with a good brocade or brochi silk.

A new ramps coat is "s ablc of being very smart wten it is short, but an additional inch or two at vac* make eit dowdy: The very latest style shows the combination of lace and fur that is so very inuch liked, and judiciously used it looks ex- tremely well. A coat of olive green cloth covered with stiiiig coloured gulnite, the sleeves and the trill being of dive wren velvet, the latter lined vti,h silk of a ligln cc tint looks well. All the fur i. rich dark ealde. The guipure over cloth is ca/ried out in the epaulettes and "bell " frills • tSiat finish tho sleeves, and these are lined with itik like the other frills.

Ail iho new mai,tles are eloped away from the n- ••14. downward,, the curve sweeping round to- m ai7l-1 the b4cic, and this allows, a little of the f• .a.t of the wattage and the waistband to be seen. Alt collars, too, are very high, so as to frame the head and leave no possibility of a breath of cold air reaching the back of the neck. A very nice fawn cloth cape edged with three rows of braid, sini having similar triplets of braid reaching quite 1., the middle of the back. The high collar is fi Je'ned and hoed with fur, and the ouble frills t on the crot,s are edged with rows of braid and lined with a considerably lighter shade of fawn cloth.
Your loving JNNEUL

div.head: U WOMEN'S CEIAT."
div.p: U WOMEN'S CEIAT."

London has been very destitute of Royal folks of late, and with the exception of a few"pas-inz through" visit promises to remain for some time yet to come. The Prince and Princess of Wales will not be at Marlborough House to stay until December, when they will in all probability, epend a week or two in town for Christmas shopping, as is their rule. The Empress Frederick, on the conclusion of her visit to Balmoral, will spend a few days at Buckingham Palace, on Ler way to Sandring- ham.

With Buckingham Palace are associated some of the greatest events of Her Majesty's life, both as Queen and woman. From there the Royal maiden went to her coronation, there her wedding breakfast was given, and it was there her lint child—the Emprees Frederick, our Princess Royal—was laid in her arena. The grounds, over forty acres in extent, are guarded f rum the eyes of the

_ tile eyes u. . - - curious, by walls surmounted by formidatle-looking spikes. Within stands the Pavilion, built during the present reign and in the biography of Her Majesty we are tsld of the great interest which she, the Prince Con- sort, and the Royal children toLls in the progress of the work. Within the walls of Friedrichshof, the residence of the Empress Frederick in the Taunus Mountains, which her Imperial Majesty has recently completed, are many otjects of art and interest. These are not only the re suit of years of indefatigable collecting on the part of the Empress and late Emperor, hut heirlooms, presents, and souvenirs of travels in different countries, and widening in a remarkable degree their tastes for, aed love of art. In a Louis XV cabinet in the library, is a selection of autographs arranged with the greatest nicety, and of singular interest. Here are preserved the handwritings of the Elchenzsllern family, of Royal personages in Great Britain, Austria, Russia, Sweden. Belgium, etc. the sign mantaala of statesmen, savants and artists, and of all who have made their mark in the world's history. Adjoining, in a flat glass case, ars gold, silver and bronze medals, representing members of the British and Prussian Royal families. In a similar case are samples of ancient keys. Their workmanship is excellent and tells of months of such patient labour as the 19th century never sees. But most amusing of all the curios is the combined spoon, knife and fork, which used to be carried about by ladies and gentlemen. The birth of a second son to the Duke and Duchess of Marlborough is said to be somewhat a disappointment ta the lather who would much have preferred a daughter. It ma lfe3 hswever, the succesaiou doubly sure, and this will probably go some way in comfortine the Duchess. The little Marquis who not long since celebrated the first anniversary of his t isthday is a bentry child,and a great , pet with his numerous relatives. The taste for sport and straight shooting would seem to be develo, ine very considerably among fashionable women. The Marchioness c f Breadalbane. and Ladte Tv eelmoutli both bring down their stage like men, and Mrs. Algie Bourke uses her rifle in a deer forest with signal success The Duchess of Bedford is an excellerit Shot with greusa and p-.rtritiges. and Lady Beaumont hie lo a taste for partridge shorting. Mrs. Efwfa Wil- liams is welt known as a good shot, and at Inoercauld, where she has teen staying with Mr.and Mrs.Newmar.n, Oh^ despatched two or three very fine stage. Ss far as tie cycling .rszs is concerned this is, among the many who tosk up the pastime simply b. cause it was the fashionable craze of the hour.almost dead. The girls and en-men who still ride do so because they really enjoy the exercise,and genuisely prefer tt.e bicycle as a means of locomotion. They would do well though t) consider carefully whethcr cycling is really beneficial to their health, Without doubt, a good deal of physical harm has resulted in its adoption by girls and women qf delicate build. Among horsewomen. Lady Sybil Primrose is a shining light, but Lord Rosebery has no desire to are her in the hunting field, and so far she has not appeared there. Lady Figgie is scarcely so good a horsewoman as her sister, but she knows no fear when in the saddle, and the sisters take this—as indeed they do all other °servile together. The tastes of the two girls are simple in the extreme. They were very quietly brought up, and there is about them a rare charm of simplicity, earoestness and freshness. Evening frocks are being msulded, as far as possible, on the same lines as walking growns. The under skirts of silk or satin fit very closely from waist to knee, and over them two or three 'ceilings of chiffon, or mousseline de sole, in colours that contrast or harmonise with em- broideries of shining paillettes or glittering tinsel en one , cf them only, and that not the outer one, are arranged. These embroideries are only visible now and again, for a moment, when their bright surfaces change to catch the light. Touches of fur are being used again this season with excellent effect upon some of the more solid sort of evening gowns, in satin and brocade. With the chance in temperature everyone has un- earthed their furs, and at the moment furriers are almost everwhelmed with work. In boas capes, and collets,the choice is bewildering, which to the impecunious is a die- tinct advantage, as it means that one can almsst.dOn almost any style and not look conspicuous. For in. lance, those of us po wailed of a tight fitting fur cape,ae worn a decade back, need only slit it up in five oral* places (taking care that an opening comes over arm) and insert in each a very full box pleat of velvett and add a moderately high box-pleated velvet collar, lined with a pleating of chiffoo, in any colourpreferred, t ) bring the ancient garment completely and delightftflry up to date. I have seen several treated so, and the effect was all one could possibly desire. Speaking of the temperature, it may interest many of my readers to know that the first thermometer was invented by a peasant named Drebbel. of Notth Holland. Drebble's thermometer was composed of a vertical glass tube, ending at the tcp in a bulb, while the lower end was plunged into a vessel filled with water, or some colored fluid. When the bulb warmed, the expanded air within it drove back the water. When the air ensiles& again, the external pressure caused the liquid to rise again ha the t be. 4 Fahrenheit, who succeeded in perfecting the mercucey thermometer, was, at one time, a merchant of Dantzic, but he was not successful, and tureei his attention to chemistry. His system of notation ie very arbitrary, and there can be no doubt that the Centigrade system invented by Celsius, which. allows a hundfed degrees between freezing and boiling point, is more satisfactory from a scientific point of view, while that of Reaurnur is widely aefopted in Franee and is practically the only system used in Russia. 'Me death of Gabriel Daniel Fahrenheit took place a little more than one hundred and sixty years ago. Good domestic servants are apparently becoming rarer and rarer,but as usual " Its an ill wind that blows no good." Mistresses can no longer get along without a personal knowledge of domestic duties, and with more frequent visits to the kitchen.better and better will be the i sanitary conditions prevalent in ttsoseereginnwand fewer epidemics in our midst. When a woman boast' that she never ha e cause to go into her kitchen " hr r maids are such treasures" the chances are that the household whee's are kept well oiled only at the expense of perfect cleanliness. It is very nice to have our dinners well reeved, but what abou'.; the saucepans and pots in willed the dinner hag been cooked ? And the cleanliness` of

inks, and the humble hut indispensable dishcloth ? Un- certainty on these points is unpardonable and danger- ous. Even if the lady of the hipme does not actually touch the preparations for dinner in the kitchen, she should understand how everything should be done so as is check waste and extravagance. So too should she be conversant with the current prices of foods and know where provisions and meets, fish and vegetables are to be had most reasonable. It is a mistaken idea to suppose that butchers' meat is the cheapest food one can put on the family dinner table. There are certain periods of the year when the housewife might provide poultry and game without being in the least extravagant and the change would be acceptable and whoh some. rOMATO Jaar.—Wipe the fruit and take off the stems, and place in a preserving kettle allowing half the weight in sugar. Ada a little water for syrup. Slice one lemon for each two pounds of fruit and add. Boil till the syrup is thick. This is an excellent preserve, and tastes like figs. " MADGE."

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH PAROCHIAL COMMITTEI4:
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH PAROCHIAL COMMITTEI4:

A meetpig of the St)cktnn Death Parechcal Committee wag held in the National Schools, Stockton Death' on Thursday last week. Mr. Davenport preziried,and there were also present :—Messrs. Pearson, Weir, Clarke, Mason, Ashton Reyes, with Mr. George Ashton (assist- ant clerk), Mr. Swinton (surveyor), and Mr. Famegtm (nuisance impector).
ILLNESS OF THE CLERK.

Mr. George Ashton reported that his father, the clerk, was ill at home, and was unabl- to be present. It was resolved on the proposition cif Mr. Pearson that Mr. George Ashton act as clerk in his absence.

THE LATCHFORD SEWERAGE ARRANGEMENT. Mr. Clarke said Mr. Pilling, was unable to be present, but he had asked him (Mr. Clarke) t) state that Latch. iird woud be wilting to agree to tbo terms stated for using the sewers of Stockton Heath provided that the extra Id. rate to be paid over and above the sewers rate of Stockton Heath ceased a'ter 30 years. Mr. Mason said he did not think that wa: ever con- templated when the terms were drawn up. The Chairman did not see that there was any thing unreasonable in the request. Stocktm Heath borrowed the money on a repayable loan for thirty years, and at the sod of that time they would have finished paying. If Latchford were willing to pay for 30 pars it was putting them on the same tams.
Mr. Mason said Stockton Heath would not get a rate over all the Latchford area as was the case in kttickton Heath. Mr, Clarke; You get the rate from all those wl” use the sewer.

Mr. Mason : In Stockton Heath all the property owners pay for the maintenance of the sewage system whereas in Latchford only a portion will do so. Mr. Clarke : That argument would be all vt ry well if you were putting their sew( rs down. Here you are paying nothing, and it is only lair to ark Latchford to pay for 30 years. The Chairman : Stockton Heath will benefit by the arrangement. It was probable that all along this road at Latchford there would be houses and they would all have to pay this increased rate. Mr. Mason said it was probable that in course of time the whole of Latchford would be draining its sewage in- to their sewer at Stockton Heath, and that great in- creaser might entail a great expense on their part. The sewers might not be large enough, whereas if they had left Latchford alone they would have been sufficiently large for Stockton Heath.
The t

Mr. Weir : Were we compelled to have Latzbford Without included in our sewage system ? The Deputy-Clerk : Yes upon certain terms. Mr. Clarke : Perhaps the Surveyor will be able to tell us whether the sewers will be large enough if we had to take the whole of Latchford sewage. Mr. Mason : He is no more competent to judge than ourselves.
Mr. Swinton : I should say the sewers would not be large enough for the whole of Latchford Without. The Chairman : I think we shall be the gainers in the long tun. . _

_ Mr. Mason : We ought to take time to consider it. It is an important matter. The Deputy Clerk said he did not think the conunitt-e was in order in discussing the matter that night. If there was to be any alteration of the terms already , agreed upon—and there was no mention of 30 years in the agreement—the initiative would have to be made by the District Council on behalf of Latchford. It was ultimately decided to adjourn the consideration of the matter until the suggestion respecting ttse pay- ment for 30 years came officially from • the District Council. THE WARRINGTON CORPORATION AND THB FAIL STsTEII. The Deputy-Clerk said the Clerk was instructed at the last meeting to ascertain if the Borough of Warrington had any power to compel prcperty owners to make use of the rail system. The Clerk bad seen Mr. Lonedinr the Borough Surveyor, and he informed him that the Borough had no byelaws or special act of Parliament to compel owners of property to adopt the pail system. They had to take each case as it arose on its merits. Mr. Mason: Does that mean that a person can please himself whether he adopts the pail system. The Deputy Clerk : The Corporation have no corn- pulFory posvem to make him do so. Mr. Farrington said the system was uniform through- out the Borough. The Chairman : We shall therefore have to try and prevail upon those who are building property in Stock- ton Heath to do as we requlro. PROPOSED CORPORATION TRAMWAYS TO STOCKTON HEATH. The Town Clerk of Warringcon wrote as follows "The Corporation propose to obtain powers to enable them to construct tramways within the Borough and they desire to ascertain the views ef your authority with respect to the construction of tramways within your district. Presumine that powers could he obtained for the construction of a tramway from the Southern bound- ary of the Borough into your district with a terminus near the Mulberry Tree Inn would your authority sup- port the application of the Corporation to construct it if they cave the uswri clause for the repair and mainten- ance of the roads." The Chairman ; That will be a mater in which the Connty Council -wilt have to be considered. Mr. Clarke said Stockton Heath pelole were quite willing to assist Warrington in anything that was reasonable, and they would no doubt be glad to have a tram:way to Stockton Heath. There WES no doubt the War rington people would construct the tramway for their own benefit. He had bad the question on his mind for a to g tirs.e of the price charged by the Warrington Corpo•ation to consunaera of gas in Stockton Heath. They compelled Stockton Heath peiple to burn the War- rington Corporation gas, and charged them sixpence yer thousand feet more than the Warrington nonsumers paid. Be thought that was an unfair position for them to be in. He was not prepared to support the Corporation in their tramway scheme that night, and he thought before the Council did so they should ins's; on a reduction in , the price of gas. It was decided that the Chairman, lairsus. Mason and Clarke form a sub-committea to go into the question and report. This concluded the business.

div.head: HE EXAMINER FRIDAY, OCTOBER 28 1898
div.p: HE EXAMINER FRIDAY, OCTOBER 28 1898
"Lod defend the richt," said 1, fervently "Nane but He can save us."

"Sandy," observed Mark, with grim humour, "I'm sick of the barley-water. Where's the whiske,? The redskins are having a spelt, B2cky dogs! ' "Ye're wrang," said I, without heeding his call for alcohol—a danger devoutly to be avoided —"look on the roof! D'ye see ony figures creeping like snakes towards us alang the parapet ? There. an' there! D'ye see?" Mark's rifle-shot was the reply, and a redskin rolled over with a sepulchral groan. Immediately after the besiegers began yelling, and both on the tower and within the Presidio we raised a shout of defiance. Yes, a British cheer disconcerted the fiends. The enemy had mustered all his strength for this combined attack, and we had to thank the 'lickness of our brick and adobe building that' we ',re not massacred at that fearful crisis, for the .ve vehemently attacked every weak spot of our last refuge. "Let such of the wounded as wish, and are able to stand the strain, be carried up the tower," ordered our leader, which was a sad signal that the end was fast approaching. "Mark, do km smell the oil ? " asked the Senorita. "They are firing the woodwork." With .that warning she and others stood ready with their 'buckets of water, and as the men used their rifles and pistols, two or three of our women threw water over 'the charring wood. Simultaneously with this attack on the basement we heard ominous noises on the roof, and this caused dismay in every breast. Alas! there appeared no hope of holding out till daylight. •In our despair we were now reckless of all danger, and this, perhaps, awed our antagonists. ' At this juncture Mark' • suggested that one half of us should protect ,the tower and roof, and the Others peck the ground, and with our spades heap the dibris over and about the barricades at the doors. This would be fire-resisting, and, anothei ambush behind which to fight. The dea commend- ing itself, the lads worked 'with hearty goodwill, and within ten minutes the roof was cleared-of those,whe were knoeking off the tiles to'fire the rafters: • • _ _

A fair show was made with the mounds, and the redskins had ceased their attack pending. the result, of the conflagration, when Mark again joined nae,, and tapping my shoulder bade me listen attentively in the direction of the north-west. A lull in the fray was welcome; but was he deceived? We put our hands to our ears to assist us in catching distant sounds. We approached the tower em- brasures, and strained our ears. "It is the bark.o' a hound!" I exclaimed. "Hark!" said he, "I hear the sound of a bugle. Sandy, I've missed Jip the last two hours." "An' the Indian guide also," said T. "Listen!' , a huntsman's horn's blowing. It comes free the direction our people would tak'. Hush a moment —our foes are listening." ' The assailants evidently heard strange and ominous winds, for there was a pause in their movements. Lucia, tired and weary, had come up with a lantern, and beckoned us to approach. She peered down at a prostrate Indian, took a pistol from his stiff fingers, and pointed 'to my initials on the stock. I recognised both the weapon and our guide. "I caught this redskin assisting the enemy to ' climb into the tower," said Lucia, "and I plunged my dagger to the traitor's heart." I drew my hand thoughtfully across my fore- head. This woman's sincerity perplexed and amazed me. Here was a revelation of Indian character. The redskin in our pay, acting as our guide, the while selling us to the enemy! The tramp of many horses arrested our attention. the deadly work below was going' on by spasmodic efforts. Then a rifle shot in the distance, fired as a signal, evidently struck terror into the besiegers' breasts, as many rushed for the ramparts and gave warning cries. We were puzzled, and a silence fell upon the besiegers. , . "Help comes!" cried Mark. "Give a cheer!" We raised a cheer of welcome, and X fired my rifle. Then our bugler sounded an alarm, and the next moment the bustle of Indians leaping to their horses and the hurrahs of our friends as they approached the fort in mad haste told us that succour had at last come for the beleaguered garrison. Salvation was at hand; and we shouted with joy. "We are triumphant!" exclaimed Lucia, tears Of. thankfulness now welling from her lustrous eyes. "Endurance is half a victory. See! our friends pursue the foe. I wonder whether Muro is among the slain ?" "If so," answered Pepys, "he has his deserts. We were almost done for. Thank God for this help! " We were snatched from the very jaws of death. Women who had borne up bravely throughout the night now fainted from sheer exhaustion. Lucia was prostrated with the reaction; and when Mark held her to his breast, I saw, him raise his eyes, and his lips moved in grateful prayer for this deliverance.

div.head: (All rights reserved.) THE
div.p: (All rights reserved.) THE
SECRET OF MARK PEPYS.
Ty FRED J. PROCTOR, Author of " Timothy Twill's Secret," "Jean
Marlou, " ``Dr. Dobbs," &c.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: This story is related by Sandy Dees, a Californian tradr: before the days of the gold rush. His employer, Mark Pepys, is in love with a Mexican girl, Lucia Diaz. Manuel Muro, a Mexican. also aepears zo love the girl, and Dees fears that he,,is plotting to take Pepys's life. He doubts the giil's good faith also. One night Pepys's store is ransacked, and a half-breed on guard is killed. There is reason to believe that Muro and a band of Indians have had a hand in the affair. Pepys tai,es an oath to revenge the half,lareed. Sandy Dees discovers that Pepys has a secret which prevents him ever returning to his native land, and the Scot tries to discovet its nature. The settlement of San Leno, besieged bv Indians, sends for help. Mark and his, friends, witli Lucia, proceed thither. San Leno is besieged, and ,Mark and his men are almost defeated.
CHAPTER IX. DISCOVERY OF A TRAITOR.

The besiegers' methods of attack were so cunning that we rightly guessed their leaders possessed a knowledge of military tactics. For example, a dash was made at the alcoves, and while our main , force was repelling them the Indian reserves seized the bodirs of tile dead, and using them as shields, threw the corpses along the walls of the Presidio. Then rushing back, they snatched pieces of resin-wood, and where spears were, not ,available poked the burning ends through the loop-holes. In this way several of our defenders received ugly burns,: and one or two severe spear thruster. There were so many redskins to fill up the gaps in their ranks that the great execution made by our sturdy and crack marksmen seemed to effect but little impression. Crash! crash! fell the Indian tomahawks upon the shutters. Smash! went an impromptu battering ram through one. We were being driven to the last extremity, for the foe swarmed about us with the ferocity of hungry sharks about, a doomed ship. The sick reloaded for us, while Mark and his men defended the alcoves with spirit, until sheer neces- sity compelled 'them to fall back inch by inch towards the big door. Few shots were fired by the enemy, his ammunition being expended, but the number of corpses thrown through the alcoves into the corridor were of rather more advantage to us than to our assailants. It raised a bit of the demon in our breasts when we discovered the bodies of some of our men served in this fashion • and so pluckily did our lad repel the attacks that. now and then the enemy fell back under cover for breath and "fire-water" to screw up their courage. We noticed that nearly on each occasion a new scheme was resorted to by the dusky besiegers, and, with several mock retreats, they endeavoured to draw us from our stronghold. But Mark, though, a sturdy fighter, was too wary a captain for this, and Father Otando had warned us of such feints. It did in heart good to see this priest, his 'face glowing with excitement, and his Spanish rapier ever being thrust forward to cover himself or save a comrade.

Never, in the history of Indian warfare, had a small number of white men resisted so long, and with such little loss. ' Mark's' prowess accounted for some of this luck, the Indians being very superstitious, and, moreover, the redskins' courage was continually stimulated with alcohol; while the livelong night Lucia and her helpers kept us plentifully supplied with strong barley- water.

"Pecos," I cried, "go up the tower and report whether all is well." , The faithful hunchback scampered ' off, 'glad to be thought so useful.' "Sandy," observed Mark, "where is Jip?" "I've no' seen him lately." "Look out; lads! Here they come in force! Muster all your strength, but don't be drawn far from the door. Now, then, dash forward with a shout ! Hip, hip, hooray! At them, lads!" The two opposing forces met with the impetus of two lines of cavalry. The skill of the white men was equal to the force of the Indians, and some well-timed shots from 'the Presidio loop-holes told home with considerable effect. Mark and his men in the corridor then tried to take advantage of the confusion to retreat within the building. The door once barred, we could hold out another hour, but our leader's voice stopped the deign. "1 noir out! Here they come again! Form up z.nd &el" •

volley gave the redskins a momentary check, but they came on again with renewed vigour. Our gallant men met them with prais3worthy steadiness, and for a couple of minutes the affray was indescribable.

"Forward, lads!" Mark shouted, as the Indians faltered a moment, and with irresistible courage they not only repelled the onslaught, but acted on the offensive with such deadly effect that the redskins lost heart and retreated pell-mell. "Now, lads, get inside! Fire as you go, to cover your retreat!"

The assailants soon perceived this stratagem, and came on again with merciless ferocity,. but Mark and his comrades were too smart for them. Each man being safe inside, the door was closed, bolted, and barred; and as thei e was no chance of hitting our people, the loophole marksmen made short work with the boldest of those who were soon battering the door. "Distribute yourselves," was our next command, "and pick off the cowardly ruffians who lead. Europeans first." "Mark! "urged Lucia, "it is---" But she half- fainted before the sentence was ended.

I could not blame our captain for this order, because the enemy gave him no quarter. Besides, without leaders, Indians are soon cowed. Lucia's fear was not incomprehensible to Mark, but, while kind to her, he never countermanded the order. Meanwhile a sturdy defence of the windows WRS necessary, for every artifice was used to effect a-n entrance that way. We all suffered a good deal from fire and smoke, and those told off to remedy the defects had to erect barriers before the door and windows with thick planks and every portable article not needed by the wounded. This lasted fully fifteen minutes, when through the smoke I caught sight of Pecos urging Lucia to ascend the tower stairs. For a moment my heart seemed to cease beating, but sterner work scared the dread. "Mark," said I, as he was holding a stool against the door, "their efforts are mair spasmodic." "Then the wretches are up to some new trick," he replied. "Lads, put your shoulders to the work. We will die game!" "Help! Help! " came the distressing cry from a woman on the tower stairs; and through the dingy atmosphere we mix Lucia waving us to join her. "Come at once, Mark, for they are scaling the . tower walls. Come quickly!" Both of us rushed to her aid, and with a bound or two Mark was at the top of the stone steps. There he stumbled over a prostrate form, but happily I was nimble, and as a treacherous red- skin, who had jumped over the buttress was about to club my friend, I ran my bowie-knife into his bowels and closed with him. By this time Mark was upon his feet, and Lucia had reached the platform. Quick as lightning she stabbed a redskin who was climbing up a long pole that rested against the top of the tower, while Mark and I had our work cut out to hurl two stalwart fellows from the stonework, where they held like a vice with their left hands and struck out at us with their tomahawks. Save for the moonlight our lives had been forfeit, but Mark's valour was equal to his immense strength, and those who managed to reach the buttress were soon burled backwards and fell upon their howling friends, or struck the stony ground with an ominous thud. 'Lucia," cried Mark, "go down quickly and send up two men, well armed, to -take our places. We shall render better service below." I' fired several shots among the besiegers without exposing myself, and when Mark followed my example we could hear the rage of the redskins because their plan was frustrated. I shudder as I write—less because the modest efforts of an old man make him conscious of a feeble pen, than by reason of the scene from that tower, which even now stands out so vividly. It was horrible work, the like of which history has not surpassed. What with the fires around, the noise of howling savages battering the doors and windows, the screams of an hysterical woman, whom neither coaxing nor threats could pacify, the groans of the wounded and the curses of some of the dying fiend, outside, the scene was more like Pandemonium than "God's fair earth." "Hold to this spot," ordered our leader, ! addressing the two men who came up at the ' Senorita's bidding. "We make our list stand here, when refuge below is impossible."

div.head: CHAPTER X. LUCIA'S vow.
div.p: CHAPTER X. LUCIA'S vow.

"Our rescuers will take in the situation at a glance," observed Mark, as he shook himself to- gether. "Let us scour the country around the fort to cut off retreat." "The Indians," I replied,"having exhausted their powder an' arrows, will fall an easy prey to our ' marksmen. The redskins hae shewn na mercy, so their stragglers will plead in vain fer quarter." "They merited heavy punishment, for their attack amounted to a massacre of innocent people. Nothing can justify their conduct." When our ardour in pursuit somewhat abated, I returned to the Presidio, to find Mark and the Senorita busily engaged binding wounds and sooth- ing the sufferers. "The reinforcements have renewed our lads' courage," observed Mark; "I've ordered a portion of them to keep strict watch, while a batch has ridden back to protect the waggoners and women and children. What's the list of our casualties ? " "No' so heavy as anticipated. So far as we ken there are eleven dead or beyond hope o' reoovery, seventeen severely wounded, an' fourteen slightly. It was tough wark. The reckless fanaticism o' the Indians enabled our bullets to play fearful havoc amang their ranks, an' their endeavour to carry the ramparts an' gates by assault cost them many lives. Six Mexicans are amang the enemy's dead; but flee sign o' Muro." You see," rejoined Mark, "we had the advan- tage of fighting under cover, and with an intimate knowledge of every inch of our hiding places. Sandy, while I think of it, just feed the smoulder- ing fires, casting sufficient glare on the fortifica- tions to enable the men to repair them. I want to help Lucia with the sick; so see to it at once, and give me a call if anything happens." The devotion of Lucia to the wounded was beyond praise, but the women of San Leno were none the less assiduous in their nursing. One or two of them had bruises, the fingers of one were jagged, and the Seilorita was suffering considerable pain from her flesh wound. Her fortitude was astonishing, for while there remained one of the . _ .

wounded uncared for she refused to rest a moment. The surgical skill of one of our party, together with the Friar's medical knowledge, did much to relieve pain. When the welcome dawn at length came the Presidio was somewhat ship-shape. This gave the patients more comfort, and their condition was further alleviated by the arrival of the waggons, which brought supplies and ambulance necessaries. My own clothes being smeared with blood and dirt, I put on my Scotch dress and kilts, Mark acknowledging that I looked "as fresh as a daisy." The rough-and-tumble contest of many of our men at wrestling quarters in the courtyard had torn their clothes very considerably. Mark's injury was, happily, only an - ugly scalp abrasion, the skull bone help- uninjured. His face was begrimed powder-smoke and dust, and the tattered i,,n of his blouse chewed how his masterful arms bad assisted in slaughtering the enemy. He was sprinkled with blood, and as the 'corning dawned he found his limbs achim,. But lie set us a good examplo by snatching a few hours' sleep. Alas as for myself, I had crowed too early, for when I woke my whole body felt az though basted; end at noon when Mark saw me hobbling .about, his first greeting was not a sympathetic allusion to .tny liver, but: "Well, Sandy,. what should we do without the women ?" "Irrational beings that they are in prosperity," I rehTied with a smile, "in adversity they certainly shine." - "You deserve to marry a shrew," he retaliated, "for your past lack of chivalry. I'm glad I was horn a man, for women have the larger share of p:in and sorrow. When good women assist us men . to iade thel'world, brute force will begin to die a

flat nral 'death." ikra'tdc and I examined the grounds, and found only two wounded Indians still breathing, the rest. ;laving ended. their own lives or crawled into the woods tc: •die. Within a semi-circle of one hundred feet r.ulins, taking the gate as a centre.

div.head: CURSI
div.p: THE CURSI

we counted eighty-seven reusxins, and within the fortifications sixty-one bodies. At certain spots our guns must have played grea havoc, for the mangled bodies lay in lines; and the dead along the path of pursuit testified to the spirit of revenge which animated our reirforePments. "Tie wonder °beer led my friend, "to see the compara- tively alma loss on our side; but much of that is accounted for by our caution and effective firing. The Indians, superstitious and cowardly, were goaded to the attack. Thank God we had no mercenary allies to shew cowardice. Each able- bodied man and woman did good service." The rosy clouds were just dispersing under the influence of a glorious sun, when a stray redskin was caught prowling like a coyote in the vicinity of the mission, and was detected in the act of plunder. Some of our people caught him red-handed, and in a trice he was hanged to the branch of a tree at a spot where his dangling body could be seen for a considerable distance, and act as a scarecrow to frighten others. After this we were not troubled by a single red man, for they crawled to cover like lizards among the "skeet" bushes, or shambled to the gulches. Precautions against surprise completed, we had a refreshing wash and brush up, and then partook of a hearty dinner. Each man told his experiences of the fight. One related how he knocked an Indian's teeth down his throat, and then. how he and his comrades piled the dead redskins between, the howitzers, and from behind this rampart re,., pelled a second attack., A wiry Mexican deserm,„ how he was clutched by a warrior in the fashion or a bear's hug, and that both" of them rolled dow"n' the rampart into the 'dry ditch. The Alexioan, managed to draw his bowie-knife with his left hand, and plunged it into his assailant's tide. The Indian then bit his shoulder, the marks of teeth being still visible. "There was considerable blood on the turf out-' side the outer wall, where we threw the broken glass," said Mark. "I've examined the feet of many of the dead in that quarter, and they are fearfully cut, showing hew the device assisted us ka defend so long against such overwhelming odds. The majority of the firearms We've found are v..y antiquated, and I lee that the explosilm of an Indian's Musket caused the owner's death." "judging by the clothing an' 'attenuated bodies o the majority o' the dead," said I, "the wretches belang to the ugly an' dirty aborigines; but there are w few' braves amang them whose looks point, to better breeding—the mair to their shame fer fighting against us. When education an' civilised surroundings do no' improve a man's tastes his heart's bad." "Still," argued Mark, "a race better housed and fed is inclined to be contented and happy. The agitators to rebellion are mostly to blzgae• But come, let us gather the spoil." After collecting all the valuables belonging to the slain, the owners were buried in graves dug iw the loose ground about half a mile from the fort, With regard to our own killed, Father Otando performed the last rites of the Church,and,contrary to the usual custom in those days, there was no feast after' the funeral. Mark sprinkled the graves with flowers as a tribute to the memory of brave men who bore adversity with cheerful resignation and courageously died at', the post of duty. Then Lucia took Kana's Royal cross from her bosom, and, gazing at it intently, kissed it, and said, with solemn earnestness: ". "At whatever sacrifice te myself, even though my heart be riven, these men shall be avenged! With lips compressed and eyes flashing she entered the sanctuary, walked firmly up the aisle, knelt before the altar, and there sealed her vow.

We set to work immediately to strengthen the fortifications,' and when all the wounded were off the sick list Mark selected discreet volunteers to join our expedition' to Golden Vale, three women accompanying Lucia. It transpired that those Indians we met on our way were worldly-wise, softening the keen edge of our resentment by offering gifts of maize and honey. And so we journeyed on our triumphal way, and 7„after many days encamped in a picturesque spot. On the second afternoon of our stay we gave ourselves up to enjoyment. Soon the woods rang with harmony of a most enticing sort, for the squirrels came forth and peaceful Indians gathered about us. "Come," airily cried our leader, "let us have healthy pleasure; it is the grease which makes the wheels go lighter. People who mope through life rob others of enjoyment, as well as themselves. Pipe away:" Responsive to the call of many voices, I gave a Scotch air on the bagpipes, and, strangely enough, this was a signal for every squirrel to retreat with ludicrous haste. Our fellows roared with laughter. I have heard travellers say that the Californian sciuridte invariably retire at the sound of mournful notes, but I was not prepared for this insult to a Scotchman's lively bagpipes. "The pibroch' stirs men to valour," said I, "but it frightens a Douglas squirrel into fits." "Compared with Lucia's charming melody," chaffed Mark, "your tunes would scare a rattle- snake."

My retort was a near approach to the profane, and then I squatted, looking on in gloomy silence. Thereupon the efficient band struck up a lively "contradanza," while the rest of them danced its intricate figures and combinations as well as the unevenness of the sexes permitted. This was followed by a stirring song about the flag of Old England, and then Mark and Lucia joined in dancing an "El jambe." Their feet were so rapid, harmonious, and precise as to sound like the gentle rattle of drumsticks in the hands of a skilled musician. _ _

The two made a striking couple; his herculean body moving with amazing sprightliness, and Lucia's grace and beauty delightfully blending with her picturesque dress. They were at the height of their hilarity, and we full of fun and frolic, when the crack of a shot, followed immediately by another, brought us to a sudden knowledge of our danger. "A pony is hit!" I cried, as one fell about fifty feet from us. Instinctively we flew to cover and seized our weapons. The Indians standing about us were puzzled, so evidently they were not a party to the dastardly surprise. Several of the men cautiously moved towards the enemy's ambush, while I examined Lucia's reboso, the fringed end of which had been pierced by a bullet. Evidently the miscreant had aimed to shootjour leader and his lady-love. "That was a narrow escape," observed Mark, somewhat bewildered. "It should teach us caution," said I solemnly, "fer we're shadowed." "Luck is with us, Lucia," he remarked. "The fellow meant to bring us both down. He intended us for fine sport, while we were as unconscious as young rooks." The whole camp was not only on the alert, but several crack shots were told off to pursue the enemy, duly taking precautions for safe retreat in case of meeting great odds. The spirit of adventure kept our minds at such useful tension that no danger scared us longer than a moment. Shortly the pursuers came back without tracing the culprit, but they said there were evidences that the enemy anticipated the services of our faithful bloodhound, Jip, for pains had been taken to completely destroy the scent along several hazardous trails in the direction from whence the shot came, and leading eastward. - "This," observed one of the men, handing an Anahuac bronze razor-knife to Mark, "I found near the spot whar the shots must hey' been fired, an', moreover, boot-prints shew that no unshod Indian made them." • ' . .

Lucia's face was overshadowed by a look of mingled fear and perplexity, her bosom heared, her breath then came and went quickly, she shuddered violently, and her lips paled as she said: "Was there more than one marksman ?"

"One only," replied the man, as he watched her dark, long eyelashes quiver upon her pale cheeks, "an' the hoofs of a mustang are plain enough until the grassy, slopes are reaChed, whar they disappear. While we cautiously worruid our way, I'll bet the would-be murderer escaped—lucky dog." "Dog!" cried Lucia vehemently, springing erect and crushing a flower in her hand. "He's fiend!" Her head was thsown back as she wildly added: "He knew Jip's powers, and destroyed the scent; therefore, he was,at'Yerba Buena." And seizing Mark by .the wrist, her whole framt trembling, and her beautiful , eyes flashing tu smitten swords in warfare, she- excitedly cried': "The man who fired those spots had some hand iz the robbery of Puke's Delight and the murder ol the half-caste labourer!" Convulsed by some hysterical passion, she hi her face in her hands, while Mark quickly examined the bronze knife, observing: "The Senorita is right, for this formed part ray collection. Crime is mostly discoverbd .10 accident." "Perhaps this knife was dropped as a 'blind P- I suggested. ' "It was either Mum the brigand," obserrei

Mark, "or— Why; Lucia, what's the matter T" He sprang to the Senorita's side in alarm sad, distress, and caught her in his arms, for she ha° fainted. On recovering, Lucia urged that we should press on. Now, 'it chanced that a squalid set of Monos, ot a tribal party closely resembling them, well. living on.tlae southern, extremity et the plain ve' ' traversed, in a diminutive gorge, and we calre upon a few of them in a wood. There was nothial, fierce about their features. They carried Wee' horse-hair ropes ropes and eagles' feathers. A clines,' clout covered their middle, and their bodies Wel smeared with dirty grease. -For ugliness an sensuality their faces were worse than those I carved on antiquities in the museum at Mexico. , "Sandy," observed Mark, bridling his_horse all signalling for all to stop, "most of these! fellows have two virtues—they can take white. neat and chew tobacco. Sling your pouch to theta. The little knot of dusky skins were shy at fillt",, and scampered a few paces away, as if my,.pour" were an explosive. But finding it harmless our signs of welcome persistent, by degrees , approached and gingerly picked up the pouch. "Ye see," said I, "they suspiciously turn it ' and over, like monkeys. Now they smell il that Darwin were here! .A.ha I the sinners • smoked an' tasted the• weed. afore. Look! they fight,fer 't 1 They remind me o' children scraill' bling fer nuts, or cackling hens after 'a choice morsel." J The unsuccessful ones held', out their hands f°f more. Thereupon Pecos interviewed them, witi. ca,ution, for he had previously ' warned us treachery. In, their strange vernacular Pee°* clumsily learnt that they were on the hunt for snakes, as a votive offering to the god who merle the rain. But what recommended itself to our humane consideration was the fact that the Great Spirit, or one of his satellites, was to he pro' pitiated by the sacrifice of a captive girl. I Just then the distant beat of drums in ther,j Indian camp apprised the few redskins near us that j they were being called to the ceremony. Thereuporr j a couple lifted a pole, to which a bag of live snateg I was strung • and, beckoning us to accompany there, I the whole Of us rode peacefully towards the mon. , "The old barbarous instincts of their race are' I not dead yet," observed Mark warmly; "this girl must be the victim of a tribal feud." "I daur say; an' it's our privilege to rescl her," said I;. but Mark shrugged his shoulders. "Senorita, let me appeal to ;you," I added ill Spanish. -"These redskins are going to tear 21. heart out of an inrocent captive girl." n "Then it is our bounden duty to release her, answered Lucia firmly. "Mark, you may look 0., stern as Cmsar, but I know you have not the hear'' of Nero. This maiden has done us no ill, that we should leave her to perish in the hands of mercilesii, Indians. Remember, at Yerba Buena you 01:)0 said, in toasting Harry Puke: 'May the sun never shine on a tyrant, 46 Nor go down on a slave.' And the good-tempered landlord said, in rept: ' My friend, Mark Pepys, vowed when he - England that the whole world should be h' country, and mankind his brethren.'" Mark's fa°e wore a wintry smile as Lucia added naivell; "Whether yourr-modesti forbade him saying more, I know not; but you pulled his coat tail, and he abruptly turned the subject. But sufficient ' said to convince me of-- "

"Do I know wlene Bootle village is ?" Thus said a Bootle borough constable and he added, "Ask me ill know the village of London ?" The genial officer firmly believed that the Liverpool reporter who asked him the question, was indulging in pleasantry at the expense )f thriving Bootle. When he was convinced of the seriousness of the interrogation he assisted the newspaper man to locate the rival Bootle, which consists of a very few houses. Having found the spot, continues the reporter, I set about investigating a mystery concerning the wife of an employee at the waterworks. This lady and her husband, Mr. W. Evans, reside at 11, Laburnutn-terrace, Boitle Village. At an early hsur during one of the dark mornings of February last, Mrs. Evans left the house hurriedly to take her husband's breakfast. This she handed to him, and was found some time afterwards in her house in

A SEMI UNCONSCIOUS CONDITION. She was revived, but fainted away again almost directly. A medical man was summoned, and he ordered the woman's removal to the hos- pital. As she was a woman of strong physical health, and as she had been suddenly bereft of speech, could make no explanation, nor move, the affair became shrouded with mystery. For a time/ IT WAS THOUGHT DEATH WOULD ENSUE. but after remaining in tho institution some weeks Mrs. Evans asked to be taken home to her husband. Recently she regained her speech and the strength of her legs, and, to the amazement of the village, has explained the msery. The following is the statement she readily made " I went out in my bare feet on the morning when I took my husband's breakfast. lam forty-six, and had never ailed, and thought nothing of running out on the cold flags without my boots. But I evidently did it once too often. When I got home again I went off into a faint, again and again, and when they fetched the doctor my speech bed gone, and the use had left my legs and the right side of my body. At the hospital they said I had had A, STROKE OF PARALYSIS. I didn't get any better there, and was so miserable that I felt I should die if I didn't get taken home. My hush ind was paving for my maintenance there and at last, although they were very unwilling, they allowed me to be taken home in a cab, still unab'e to speak or walk." " How did you come to get your strength and speech back, if the doc- tors could not cure you 2" " That is the wonderful thing, and the thing which I am sc. grateful. Whle I was in the hospital I thought if I had to die I might as well die in comfort in my own home, and it was after I had been at home a few days that my husband bought a box of Dr. Williams Pink Pills for Palo People. I derived almot immediate benefit from these pills, and BEFORE I HAD FINISHED THE FIRST BOX A could speak, with the exception of a stammer. I have gone on taking the pills, my sceech has coins entirely back to me, and though I am a heavy woman I can walk about almost as well as formerly, and my right arm, which had become lifeless, I can I;ft over my breast now.,

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE —THE DEATH OF MR. CHARLES TWISS. The Committee considered 135 applications for chil- dren under 13 years of age to sit for the Labour Examination to be held en the 28th inst., and:granted permission in 108 cases. It was also resolved " That this committee deeply regrets the death of Mr. Charles Twiss, which occurred on the 16th inst., and desires the Clerk to convey to the members of Mr.Twiss's family the heartfelt expression of sympathy with them in their bereavement." Councillor SHAW GREEN, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, refered to the labour examination, and said it was heartrending to have to listen to applica- tions for children who were under age to enter. ' Councillor Wows, in seconding, said that during the fifteen days the exhibition at the Gymnasium had been I opened the attendance had reached 14,516 up to the pre- vious night. (Hear, hear.) The sum of money taken in round figures was £350. That would speak for itself with regard to the interest shown in the exhibition, and I also showed that are.irrington people could rise to an &Walla enthusiasm as well as a musical enthusiasm. Councillor TINNION . How much did you take:at Parr Hall on Sunday ? Couneillor Woons : After paying all expenses we netted 31e. Counciller Ceoserene3 remarked that the cencertis on Saturday nights had been splendidly attended, and he thought it would be a great pity if the Saturday night concerts were not continued. It was most pleasing and gratifying te see the young men of the town go thotoe listen to manic instead, periling of wandering about streets or staying in Public-houses. He was at Parr Hall on Saturday night, and it really was a splendid sight to see the Hall filled. He hoped something would be done to continue the concerts. He believed there had been such concert; for two years. Cumeillor Sinew GREEN : And ought to be again. The CHAIRMAN : The Parr Hall Committee have :e under consideratlon,and they will do all they can in the matter. Alderman Surron endorsed the remarks of Councillor Crosfield and thoueht concerts should be held through the week whenayer the Parr Hall was disengaged, and the price for admisaion put at a very low figure. Counciller Snew GREEN referring to the opening of the exhibition on Sunday, said he was astounded when- he saw the announcement, issued, so , far as he was aware,without any meetin,g of the committee to sanction the opening. He did not think the working people, attended. It Was simply an opportunity for young people te meet there. COM:Miner WOODS No sir. Councillor SHAW GREEN: It was very strongly im- pressed moon me from what I saw. anfrdom decidedly the commence. mc) ntr a eCuetutnocitihl oer dict that statement. fiWri iOsOhDasnd dwi satsi ntchtel yr 9 Councillor Snew GREEN : lam not going to propose a resolution. I simply express my conviction that such a course was an unwiee one. , Alderman ROBERTS said that when Councillor Shaw Green called into question the action of the sub-commit- tee in opening the picture exhibition he fait he could not allow his :pullers to go by unchallenged. He would nut this b,nad and simple question to anybody who ob- jected to the Sunday opening of a picture exhibition, and ask him to define what law of God or man was broken by an individual whn took advantage of the op- portunity to look upon a beautiful work of art? (Hear, hear.) When he got an answer to that qeestion he would discuss the matter further. (Hear, hear.) Couneillor TINNION, in proposing the confirmation of the minutes of the Gymnasium Committee, said the committee distinctly disencieted themselves from the 'Arts Committee in opening their exhibiticn on Sunday. He did not knew with what license they held it. The Gymnasium Committee were not consulted in the matter. The CHAIRMAN I ter derstand the committee would Much rather see men going there than into a publio- -1 house. (Hear. hear.) Councillor Treneroze : The public-houses were not open at that time. Alderman RousaTs said as one of the three members comprising the sub-committee—the other two members being Councillor Woods and Councillor Crosfield— he was fully prepared to take his share of the responsibility, and, if necessary, to justify his action on proper and reasonable grounds. They were indebted to the Gymnasium Committee for allow- ing them the use of the bailding, but after they had got that, they did no think it necessary to aek the permis- sion of that committee while they used it for the purpose for which it Was lent. Councillor TINNION Sail his contention was not with regard to the opening of the exhibitioe, but with regard to the charge made for admission. lithe committee had known this, teee- would very likely have refused per- mission. Alderman ROBERTS : The Chairman of the Gymnasium Committee was present at the meeting of the sub-com- mittee and consented to the opening of the exhibition on 'Sunday. The minuees were passed. QUEEN'S GARDENS CRITICISED. Couneillor BENNETT refers, d to the opening of the Queen's Gardens said he had heard some very out- spoken criticism of the arrangement of the gardens, and more particularly of the lamentable dearth of trees. There were magnificent asphalt walks and an ornate and richly decorated fountain, and while he had no objec- tion to them he thought the gardens should be made more private by the planting of trees. The CHAIRMAN : They could not plant trees in the middle of summer. Councillor BENNETT : Autumn is the proper time and it should be done now. Coencillor TINNION said ho had heard complaints about the children running about the gardens on Sun- day, and thought it was not the intention that the gar- dens should be used as a playground. Alderman SUTTON said be never did appreciate the gardens. Instead of being called Queen's Gardens they should have been called Baby Gardens. (Laughter.) He had heard, however, of people using the gardens as a short way from nne street to the other, and suggested the advisability if closing the gates. . Councillor TINNION It is a great convenience. The Cum mean : Why shouldn't they? They do so in other towns. Alderman SUTTON : I object to it, and that is why I have brought it forward. I wilt bring it before the committee at the next meeting. The CHAIRMAN : I don't think that you will get it carried. Councillor HEATON replied and hoped the members wool] make as many complaints as they could. (Laughter). THE PRInE OF GAS BY SLOT METERS. Councillor FURNESS aske i the Chairman of the Gas Committee whether it was ths intention of the committee to make any concession to users of penny-in-the-slot meters. It seemed to him that these people were well deserving of their attention. They pad ready money for the gas and there were no bad debts. The Cememete said it had been a sore point with the committee because they did not think they were being repaid for the trouble of collecting the coins, but the people would have the reduction as soon as it could be given them. The minutes were passed. THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY AND THEIR OBLIGATIONS. At a meoting of the Rivers Committee it was resolved that the Town Clerk write to the traders and manufac- turers using the river, informing them that the Man- chester Ship Canal Company bad been served with notice under Clause 6 of the agreement of April, 1896. and calling their attention to the provisions of the clause. Alderman ROBERTS in moving the confirmation of the minutes of the Rivers Committee, said that the clause referred to provided that if the Ship Canal Company failed to maintain the channel of the river in the con- dition referred to in the agreement the traders and manufacturers of the town had the right of navigation on the Ship Canal free of toll until such channel was properly dredged and maintained. It was not for the Rivers Commit'el to advise the traders of Warrington what action to take, but the committee called their attention to the eff eel: of tho clanse, and unless the Ship Canal Company proceeded vigorously to carry out their legal respoesibility in this matter it would not surprise him (Mr. Alderman Roberts) if the Ship Canal Company found themselves confronted by a considerable amount of trouble which would be raised by tie traders of War- rington in regard to the payment of tolls which they might or might not be exempted from by the conditions which at present obtained. Councillor PIERPOINT seconded. Alderman HARRISON, in supporting the confirmation of the minutee, said the Ship Canal Company had no firmer friends than the Corporation of Warrington in the furtherance of their sell me, and it appeared to be very ungracious on the part of the Company to pursue the course they were at present taking. He hoped the Rivers Committee would not spare the Ship Canal Com- pany in the lent degree in keeping them steadily to their promises and insisting upon Warrington having its rights. (Hear, hear.) The MirlUtPS Were then passed. THE INCREASED DEMAND FOR WATER. PROPOSED NEW WORKS. The Water Committte stated that they had received the revert of Mr. Jamee Mansereh on the proposals of the Corporation to obtain are increased supply of water for both domestic and manufacturing purpases, and Mr. Mansergh having advised tho construction of a new reservoir in the southern part of the district of supply, and an extension of the works at Winwick, it Was re- solved that the Town Clerk be instructed to obtain the necessary powers for the construction of the proposed works. Councillor LEE, in proposing the confirmat'on of the minutes, said the report was simply of a preliminary character. Councillor SHAW GREEN seconded,and said the matter was an important and absolutely necessary one to in- troduce. In renly to Alderman Harrison, The Tower CLERK said the proposed increased supply wag in consequence of an increased coneumption. Alderman HARRISON : It is satisfactory to know that. Cenneillor Bierremer : Is it to he supplied from Win- wick ? Toe TOWN CLERK said the main proposal was to have a reservoir on the Cheshire side of the district, in order that the manufact irers of Warrington would have more water for trade purposes and at a reduced cost. This would save the Win wick water for domestic purposes. Alderman Ronears said the demand be manufacturers had increased to such an extent that the present supply was practically all taksn. The demand was likely to increase, and it was the ditty of the Water Committee to anticipate that demand. The population was increasing and the present source of supply was not sufficient to meet the poseibilitiee of the next ten or 20 years. It would be little short of criminal for the committee to allow themselves to be overtaken. Councillor HEATON asked if they had not power to purchase water under the Vyrnwy scheme for 61. Alderman SUTTON : We have that power. Coencillor LEE Raid they hoped by the new scheme to he able to sell at 61., and not buy it for 6d: ; but they could not go into details at present. - Councillor CROSFIELD remarked that the question was Of ymeirnyen importantth East the people there. An increase in the water supply of ofilelmanl ldnodne da ntdr' tthl:e rseurffe enrti nwerast eorf Warrington would be a great help te the manufac- turers, and would enable the Corporation tollsopplv at a cheaper rate. It would also encourage manufacturers to come to the town. (Hear, hear.) The DEPUTY-MAYOR : That is the main object of the committee. Councillor LONOTON asked for an estimate of the cost. Councillor LEE replied that he could not give the in- formation that night. Councillor LONGTON said it PO,MOI to him that the committee had received a report,and the result was that the Town Clerk hod to obtain the necessary powers for the con,truction of the rese-veir. If they passed the minutes that night the matter would pass out of their bands as a Crepe-11 to a large extent. Councillor SHAW GREEN : Not at all. Councillor LONOTON lam truly surprised that this should pass and that we should entertain it as we have done without having some estimate. Councillor LEE ('0 the Town Clerk) : I think we are not pledq.ing ourselves to anything p The TOWN CLERK. rPnlind in the negative. Councillor LEE : Then I have nothing to answer. The TOWN, CLERK T,R, i the following letter which he bad forwarded to Mr. White with reference to the above named matter :--"Town Clerk's offica,Warringten, 22nd October, 1896. Dear si”,—Slutchers'-lane Bridge. Mr. Stevenson estimates the cost of conetructine the author- ised road upon the company'a land at £B4O, which he has given us credit for in arriving at the sum of £1,280, the cost of widening the bridges. If the company spend the £B4O towards making the new rnad over NOW land the company will have to be nail £2,120. LYON WHITTLE. John White, Egg., Moore Hall. Warrington." The DEPUTY-MAYOR proposed the confirmation of the Minutos of the General Purposes Committee, and observed that Mr. White had agreed to the terms mentioned so far as he was concerned, but be had to bring the matter before the truetene. div.head: MAYOR THANKED FOR HIS SERVICES.
div.p: THE MAYOR THANKED FOR HIS SERVICES.

Alderman HARRISON moved "Thai the beat thanks of this Council be pre-ented to John Edward Wright, Esq., Alderman of thia Borough, tor the satisfactory manner in which he has discharge I the responsible d sties devolving upon him as Mayor and Chief Magistrate of this Borough during his year of office, and for the unvaryin courtesy and impartiality displayedby him when presiding over the deliberattoas of the Coun- cil, and in his intercourse with its members." He re- marked that he moved the resolution with considerable pleasure, though he did so with regret when he remem- bered the illness of the Mayor, whom t sey would have liked to have seen yresent. (Hear, hear.) There was not a gent'emaa present who did not sympathize most deeply with the Mayoreas and the family in the affliction which had overwhelmed them, but he was glad to learn that the extent of the illee;s had been very much exaggerated. It was pleasing to know that the conse- quences in all probability would mot be so serious as anticipated. He dared say some one would take advan- tage of the opportunity to express to the Mayor the deep regret they felt for him in his present position. The greatest dramatist the world had ever seen or heard, and whe was now peacefully sleeping his last sleep in Stratford Church, had given utterance to the words that to gild refined gold, and paint the lily, is wasteful and ridicu. bus excess. As he did not wish to lay himself open to a charge of that kind, he would add few wards to the resolution he had to submit,which fully embraced every- thing it was necessara to say about the Mayor. Alderman BLACBRURST seconded the motion, which, r; said, needed no words from him to commend it to the support of the Council, especially after what Alder- man Harrison had said. About twelve months ago he had the honour of seconding the resolution for the ap- pointment of Mr. Wright as Mayor of the borough. It was predicted then this his practical knowledge and attention to his duties, and his courtesy, would endear him to every member of the Council. That had proved to be the Case, not only S 3 far as that Chamber was concerned, but outside it. The resolution spoke for
itself. Aldermon ROBERTS supported the motion, and es- .. . . . . .

- pressed his deep sympathy with the Mayor and Mayor- ess in the very trying time they had gone through dar- ing the past few days. The members of the Council were pleased to find that the ailment from which the Mayor was suffering had been very much exaggerated. and he hoped he would be shortly res:ored to his usual state of health. (Hear, heir.) Alderman SUTTON remarked that he hoped the state- ments which had been made with regard to the Mayor would be realizad, and that he would be able to get up in a very few days. They all regretted his absence, particularly at that time ; it would have been far pleasanter if Alderman Wright could have been present to listen to the iemarks which had been made about him. (Hear, /var.) Councillor TINNION expressed the hope that they would so)n see the Mayor with them sgain. (Heir, hear.) Alderman Flurcimstax observed that not two hours ago he had the oomforting assurance that the illness of the Mayor had been very much exaggerated. There was rrason ta believe that in the course of a few days his. Worshin would be as well as he was a few days ago. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN said he had a me,sag,e from the Mayor ,to convey. as wished him to say how sorry he was he was unable to be present, and to thank the members for th&r kindness durin.; his year of office. He also wished him to convey to the officials his thanks for the valuable assistance they had given him—to the Town Clerk, ' Borough Treasurer, Borough Surveyor, and others. He (Alderman IFairclough) wished he had been there to ex. press all he felt. The Town Clerk would c nave, to him their expression of opinion. (Hear, hear.) The motion was then put, and unanimously and heartily agreed to. The Council then rose.

div.head: OUR LOCACCH.URCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCACCH.URCHES.
WYCLIFFE CHURCH, BEWSEY-STREEL

The Rev. John Yonge preached a special sermon on Sunday evening at the Wycliffe Church, Bewsey-street. The subject of the discern se was " Oa the rocks and off the line : wrecks on sea and land," and the text was part of Psalm lxxiii. 19, " Brought into des 'anon as in a moment." Th s preacher spite of the num-rous calamie ' tio s which had occurred by sea and land during the last week. In drawing Isms from them ho s tid it seemed to him that th -ise tragic events a'l combined to illustrate how when the right course was departed from disaster of one kind or other was certain to follow. If there shou'd happen to be a precipice he would advise them not to try to he clever and see how near they could get to it. If there wen rocks in their way keep off as far as possible. How many promising lives had been lost in the journey and voyage of life simply because men and women had toen careless, reckless, misguided ? They Could see these wr icks, hundreds of them on the streets of their towns and cities. Others were hidden away in hospitals. in asylums and in prisons. It was the old Story. Nuenbi:rs of these human wrecks were once as comely vessels as any of them. Many of them were those who at the start had everything in their favour— happy homes, good pareats, careful education and reigioua training. But when toey got away from home restraints and out in life, they showed complete ignor- ance of how to steer a safe course and simply went ahead as if shoals, sandbanks and rocks were things unknown and unreal. The pro +cher proceeded to speak of some of the " toidrs " in life, and said seety lay in keeping the greatest possible distance. In conclusion the preacher said if there were any in that company who were on the rocks, he point° i them to the salvation of Jesus Christ who was ready and willing to res-ue them. WYCLIFFE teS.A. SOCIETY. " "

At the meeting of this society on Sunday afternoon the chair was occupied by Mr. William Hickman, the president of the P.C.A. Society at the Y.M.C.A. Rooms. He spoke of the pi, mure it gave him to be present Once again at a meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. He urged the membt.rs to tale an intetest in and feel their own per- sonal responsibilt 7 for the soccoss of the rociety. The member tip could easily be largely increased if each member would use his influence in that direction. The world would never ho broeght to Christ unless those whi took upon thems.loes Christ's name laboured for it and showed the spirit of the Master. In regard to the P.S.A. movement be did not think Wtrrington had seen the trut strength of the P.S.A. He should like to see Parr HAI crowded every Sunday afternoon with mm. If someone would take It up and show an interest in it he would be the one to help.—The addrers for the a'ternoon was delivered by Mr. Wylde, of Doper Mill. fIo hasrd his remarks upon the words "Certainly I will b. with The" and delivered a most intaresting, and inAructive address.—Mr. A. Griffiths gave an excellent interpretation of the solo " Glory to Thee my God. Toe service was also tak'u part in by Mr. T. Wallington (hon. secretary), and Mr. William Beswick.
