div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
OCTOBER 28th 1898.
IT 18 ROW definitely and Mr. Gladetoae's Life. authoritatively stated that

Mr. JOHN MORLEY has been selected as Mr GLADSTONE'S biographer. We have alwai s thought the selection inevitable from the time Mr. MORLEY began to pay periodic visits to Harwarden, and to assist the statesman, whose death we all deplore, in the arrangement of his letters and papers. If anyone is capable of doing justice to the many-sided features of Mr. GLAD- STONE'S character Mr. JOHN Moaralv is the man. No person living could be selected who would com- mand more general acceptance; and yet there may be some religious men who would rather the religious side of Mr. GLADSTONE'S character were loft in other hands. Probably they are in error in believing that any lack of appreciation will be manifest in this respect. Mr. MORLEY has in living intercourse seen what his chief was like, talked with him on the highest themes, and loved him none the less because he could not agree with him. We may be sure that he will not be unjust to this side of a noble charac- ter. In other respects we may look to Mr. MOBLIT for a study of the man and his times, and his col- leagues and his opponents, that will be of perman- ent value as a contribation to the history of this country in the nineteenth century.

It has been said that Mr. MoatEr will retire from active politics in order to devote himself to the work of writing a life that must occupy him for some years. It may be true. The materials for a long and comprehensive biography of Mr. GLADSTONE are immense. Mr. GLADSTONE has arranged his documents ,by years in specie cabinets, and the letters he received from the QUEEN are to be counted by hundreds. The abundance of material is likely to be an embarras- ment. It may be necessary to call in assistance and even to hand over parts of the work to ex- perts. What we all desire is that the work shall be well done, by a conscientious as well as an accomplished writer, who will be able to analyse motive and character, as well as pen a stately narrative and picture scenes of imperishable Par- liamentary interest. Mr. MORLEY was not in Parliament in the days of Mr. GLADSTONE'S groat Budgets. He may be especially tried by the financial side of his work. But on these points assistance can be obtained without detriment to the vivacity and picturesque character of the Life. On more recent questions of Imperial policy, Mr. MoaLar was Mr. GLADSTONE'S confidant and friend. Here we may expect much that is new, but it must be years before, with the greatest expedition, the Life can reach these topics. The volumes will be published, in all probability, as they are complete. There must be at least half a dozen of them, and the interest they will excite will equal what was stimulated by Macauley's History of England and Kinglake's Crimean War, which appeared volume by volume until complete. Otherwise, we might have to wait for four or five years before beginning our new studies of a great Life.

SITUATIONS, attitudes, dramatic Mir- TheF Crisis prises, Ministerial crises, and waves of popular excitement that bewilder rance. everybody, constitute the politics of France, re- duce her to a position of weakness, and create dangers for Europe. French politics are always vivid and interesting, if they are not always Intel- ligible and rational. The present crisis is not about Fashoda, it is said to be not even about Dreyfus. It is combination against M. BRISSON, who is accused of not having sufficiently defended the army. But as no one has attacked the army, except in connection with the conduct of the Staff officer and the Dreyfus case, we cannot under- stand the accusation, except as indicating that a military dictator would be more acceptable just now than a civilian Government. To find the dictator is no easy matter, and whilst he is being sought for or is pushing his way to the front the common sense of the people may be aroused and the Republic may be saved. The formation of a new Ministry will take some time, and before it can meet the Chamber some decision raay have been arrived at which will remove the Dreyfus case from the category of political causes of excitement. The effect of the crisis on Europe must be considerable, because it seems to indicate that there is a lack of stability in the present system of government, that excitements of this kind lead on by insensible gradations to war, and that the revolutionary spirit is once more manifesting itselt in Paris and amongst the political groups of the chamber. The one fear is that the supreme direction of affairs may pass into the control of the military party, which has but a single idea—that of preventing any re-trial of the Dreyfus case. If that were to follow, there would be a momentary pause—and then? Well, we can hardly say what would happen next. Few Frenchmen care to look so far ahead. They prefer the personal conflicts and political turmoil of the time. If, however, the vindication of the army should also comprise the maintenance of Major MARCHAND, there will be war—and war with England. Happily, this conclusion has not

been made evident by anything which has hap- pened up till now. It may not occur. The deep excitement generated by other matters may re- strict the crisis to purely internal affairs, and by , the time the new Ministry is ready to face the Chamber a calmer and more pacific spirit may pr e- vail. The new Ministry, however, will have to make some declaration on the Fashoda business, and we shall probably have to wait until it is made before we can see what is immediately ahead. A new Government could as easily retire MARCHAND as it could resolve to keep him where he is. Tho probability is that it will find some way out of the difficulty, and be applauded for doing so on the plea that other matters demand attention, and that the safety of the Republic requires abstinence from external provocations and troubles. A mili- tary revolution, on the other hand, would mean war &lout Egypt generally.

Of the five Conservative candidates who are be- ing opposed in the Warrington municipal election three are directly concerned in the drink traffic, and one was a licensed victualler until a few years ago. We feel that this fact ought not be lost sight of by the electors, especially considering the way in which matters affecting a license have been recently dealt with in the Council Chamber. For years now" the trade" influence has been far too dominant in questions touching the public welfare, which have necessarily to be dealt with by the corporate body. Looking at the subject broadly no one should have any difficulty in perceiving the unwisdom and unfairness of any one branch of trade being represented to a greater extent than another, but when that trade happens to be the iniquitous drink traffic then the evil is immensely greater. Fair and unbiassed action on some questions of vital importance is impossible with such a dead weight of liquor interest in the Council Chamber. We hope that the common- sense of the electors will prevail over other con- siderations on November Ist, and that the party which has lent its support to men who are allied to the drink traffic will receive the rebuff it richly deserves.

Mr. John Sampson is doing his best to persuade the electors ot Latchford Ward that he could re- present them better than Councillor Luke Ellison —which we do not for a moment believe. His election address, "blue "in tint and tone alike, is a precious document. After the usual remarks about sanitation, paving, lighting, and economy, Mr. Sampson adds "your interests and mine are idei,tical." This is rather an elastic phrase. It might mean anything. For instance Mr. Sampson, being a publican, we presume has considerable in- terest in the sale of intoxicating drink, and the only reason why he should say the electors' interests are identical with his own, as far as we can see, is that they help in the consumption of the said drink. Many of the ratepayers who have votes to dispose of in Latchford Ward will be in- clined to doubt whether their interests and Mr. Sampson's are identical, and they vria certainly prefer to " plump " for a well-tried man like Coun- cillor Ellison rather than add to the already too strong drink representation on the Council.

Messrs. George Newnes and Co., in advertising the November number of the "Wide World " Magazine make the followhig allusion to "Louis de Rougemont." "It now turns out that his real name is Henry Louis Grin, and that it is not possible for him to have been thirty years among the savages as stated." The story, they leave to the public "to believe as much or as little as they please." After the revelations which have been made concerning this adventurer, we imagine that there is very little in his absurd story that the public will " please "to believe. For our part we shall be glad to see the last of this tissue of lies, which have not even the merit of being well told, and do no credit to the magazine which pub- lishes them.

The new circular issued by the Local Govern- ment Board in regard to the Vaccination Act sup- ports all that Mr. Chaplin and Sir Henry Fowler said in the closing debate last session. There is no intention by this measure to make it easy for the negligent to escape their responsibilities. Vaccination will still be enforced, except in the case of the conscientious objector,and the indiffer- ent will find that the process of obtaining relief is not so convenient as permitting the operation. The latter will be performed in the home ; the former must be obtained in the police-court or petty sessions at a considerable loss of time. Al- though the conduct of proceedings against de- faulters has nominally rested with the Boards of Guardians, yet the vaccination officers have from their aopointment always had direct authority from the Local Government Board,and are able to act independently of the Board that pays them. On the other hand, in case they are slack the Local Government Board has given the local boards directions to see that they perform their duty; and so a double effort is made to maintain the Act. In seine instances this will no doubt lead to fric- tion. Where a vaccination officer acts in other capacities for a Board of Guardians who are opposed to vaccination in any shape or form, he will have a hard time. But, however unpopular it may make him, he must remember that the Board above is supreme.

div.p: WARRINGTON,
CHILD'S SUDDEN DEATH AT WARRINGTON.

Last Wednesday week, the seven weeks old child of Hannah and Joseph Bradshaw, 37, Lord Nelson-street, was found dead in bad. The parents retired to bed just before midnight on Tuesday, and the eon, Joseph, slept between them. The mother awoke about 5.10 the next morning and found her son dead on her arm. Mr. Jones (deputy coroner) held an inquest on Saturday at the Police Parade Room touching the death. A verdict of " Death from suffocation due to over-laying " was returned.

The Rev. H. Brierley lectured on " Plant tissues." at the second meeting this session. There was a good attendance. Prefacing his remarks with some general observa- tions on the parallelism in structure and function between plants and animals which are alike, and the more complex manifestations of one elementary substance, protoplasm ; he showed by a series of beautiful lantern slides the origin and growth in stem, root and leaf of the various structural layers, the tissues, and of their constituent elements, the cells, as revealed by the microscope. Several mem- bers took part in the discussion which lollowed,and whilst congratulating Mr. Brierley on his perform- ance, concurred in the hope that he would continue his botanical studies on the scientific lines he has hitherto followed, and at a future dats give the club the benefit of them in another lecture,dealing rather with the actual work done by the various living plant cells than with the mere details of ulti- mate vegetable anatomy, interesting though these in themselves undoubtedly are. WARRINGTON CHURCH SOCIETY. . . .

A lecture in cannecCi;r:Wittr-ltiO".";bove was delivered on Monday evening on " The historic re- lations of the Church of England and the Church of Rome," in the National Schools by Mr. W. E. Helm, special lecturer for the Church House Com- mittee. The Rector (Canon Willis) presided. There was a fair attendance. The lecturer spoke of the character of the Church of England, its historic life and the relation of the Church of England and the Church of Rome. He said it was a fallacy to sup- pose that the Church of England was in some sense a secession from the Church of Rome. In fact, the opposite was the case. The lecturer spoke at some length on the Reforma- tion, said that the Roman schism dated from 1170, and observed that that would remain so until Rome returned to the Catholic truth and Catholic princi- ples, for the Church of England maintained and would maintain that independence as a National Church—he did not mean the modern sense—be- cause if her conaection with the State were severed tomorrow she would still be a National Church in the truest and highest sense in which any church could be national. A vote of thanks was passed to the lecturer for his able and interesting address.

RUGBY FOOTBALL.

Saturday was wet. By Jupiter ! haw it rained. second flood seemed well on the way during the greater pArt of the day. It rains in Warrington ccJagionallyr and the dew might be said to have ban gently fa:ligg the town on Saturday, but it was nothing to what visi experienced when the Warrington team reached 113ch- daleliere,the water came down in a regular deluge. You may have heard, perhaps, of the Torrent Walk. near Beige-. but you probably are entirely unacquainted with the torrent walk at Rochdale. lam not. Tne Jour. n-y from the station to the Hornets' ground was a genuine torrent walk-5a fact there was much more tot. rent about it than there was about the original Torrent Wa:k when last I saw it.

There were three of us—pressmen—and a crowd a spectators numbering ri, any as many, mad in o , gallant but soaking band, we splashed along the bill tat) streets of Rochdale. Half-way down the side of one set paved mountain we h ,ppened on the scene of ea aecirknt There was a cab wrong end up, fund brAtm shaf s and panels, arid a d .jected te king, n being drawn from out the debris. The " been haled off to some rnsdicli 11 man or other to ha his injuries attended to, while the wreck was left uncared f.,r and alone I don't know how it happened. but tiers seemed every prubability that the freshet do the hill hat been too strong for the horse.

Warrington's object was to rob a Hornet's nest-4 dangerous proceeding at any time but doubly so whet; the Hornets have b^en robbPd previously by other marauders. Nevertheless the Rochdale stronghold wa.lf successfully loctsd and without any unpleasant expsri• roes of the Hornets' sting. Perhaps the sting was out of erder owing to water haying got into its bfarings,which quite likely. At any rate it faded to act. in p!alo English the Warrington team actually won away fronl home, and cams back two points better off. This if thing they do not do more than twice in a season as I rule, and seldom at Rochdale,but on Saturday they as' tonished everybody by their success. The victory is all the more creditable as the state of the weather and the ground, made the game anybody's from start to finish.

Football enthusiasm is not dead by any means in Rochdale. Some 2,000 spectators braved the fury atlas heavens to watch the strife below. Most of them were on the ground,but not all. TW3 or three hundred econo- rnic‘l folk occupied a knoll which overlooked the field. and without paying any " tanner " had a good view Of the game. This is rather rough on the club. The treasurer should rend the hat round the slopes of that hillock, and if there is no response get a gatling gui esti the economical ones dervishes, and act Omdtarcos over again.

Alter five minutes play some of the players assumed ,an aspect that I h 4 'sea before—at Huddersfield last winter but one. They had no Bstley to meet thie time, and rather less slutch to face, but a few of the Warrington lads were nearly unrecognisable after their fret or second tackle. The Captain received particular attention and looked more like a splash of mud than any thing else. Up to ginner time there had ben a lot of punching about, scrambling, and wallowing in the wet, but no score. Then W. Rigg poised the heavy, sodden ban and cleverly droppsd a goal, thereby doing a good 1 thing for Warrington. Up to new the visitors bad shown none too much anxiety to score, but when thel found themselves two points behind,they began to make the Hornets hum. Several good attempts at passing went wrong owing to the greasiness of the ball. Louie ' Rigg cleared his lien miraculously on at least two (secs. Moog, but finally Holcroft put the finish to a combined movement by racing in at the corner. There was much 'of a give and take charaoter aftsr this, but Warrington stuck to tueir one point lead up to half time.

The second half wa pretty much the same. For the first qu•rter the visitors bad all the game, aril hard lines thrown in.pallain and Ho!croft just failed to score tries, the former after a brillant punt and dribble te the line. Then the soectators began to get :eremitic, and express their love fir He losers in no measured t.irnas. The consequence was that the Hornets ber• Warrington back and began to look earnestly for a soil Wiles to sting in. And they found it not. Warrington' armour was impenetrable to all sting, and though exceedingly hard pr.( sled they maintained their line intact to 'ha close. In the last Le! minutes, W. Meg dropped at goal but just failed to the soft place over the cross-bar, and hit one of the posts. There was a great cheer, for the ball seemed t° take a long time to travel tawards the goal, but a gross followed when it rebounded into play. The afzarnble for that ball when it drcpped was a sight to see. Thirty players went for it at once, and all got it, with the re; suit that they was a hillock of arms, lege, bodies, es' mud suddenly formed. When order had been restored It was found time to blow the whistle, which gr. ICCutcheon did, and the panting teams retired to th° dressing rooms.

RUNCORN AUXILIARY BIBLE SOCIETY, The annual meeting of the Runcorn Auxiliary Bible Society irak held at the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom. on Thursday evening, under the presidency of Mr. 25muel Taylor, J.P. There was a good attendance. wile annual report was submitted. and addreiscs well Celivered by the Deputation from the parent society. POOR RAM IN RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT. OR Saturday, the Runcorn magistrates confirmed the Making of the following poor rates :—Aston-by-Sutton, Is in the £., to produce £226 15s Id ; Aston Grange, le 4d, to produce £36 12. 81 ; Sutton, 1s 4d, to produce £440 15s 4d ; Haltoo, is 41; to nroduce £321 14s; Steck- ham, is 3d, to produce £43 4s FM "PREPARING FOR WAR AT WIDNES." lii accordande with a notice which had been issued, the Widnes corps of the 2nd Volunteer Battalion Mouth Lancashire Regiment assembled at the Drill Hall,Widnes, On Saturday, at 3 15 p.m., for mobilisation purposes. The company marched down to. the river, and went through a few movements. They then returned to the Drill Hall and dispersed 'the officers in attendance were ---Major Lewis, Lieutenant H. 11. Lewis' Sergeant-In- structor Rolle', and Sergeants Juner and D werryhouse.. DEATH OF M. GEoRGE ROBERTS. Mr. George Roberts, of Greenway-road, Runcorn, died On Sundae, after a prc tract( d illness. Deceased who Was in his .50th year, was an old and trusted employe of Messrs. Simpson, Device and Co., and wee highly res- Pected by a large circle of acquaintances. For the last ten months he had beers confined to the house, and hi demise was not altogether unexpected. He had grad- ually failed in health since he received a stroke of Paralysis some few ye irs ago. ANOTHER " ANTI-VACCINATOR." At the Runcorn Petty Sessions,on Monday, John Hail. Wood, of 613, Belfourstreet, Runcorn, applied for a cer- tificate of exemption under the Vaccination Act. He stated that he had had six children vaccinated, and he had seen id-effects from it. Toe oldest child broke out witheezema after he was vaccinated, and he had buried three since. Lie had plenty of proof that before vaccin - tion his children had been the" bonniest "in the town. The Chairman said the certificate would be granted on 'Payment of the usual fee. SUDDEN DEATif OF A Ncoase AT RUNCORN. On Friday evening Isabella Bland, seed 42 years, a nurse from Liverpool, di,d suddenly at the house of Mr. Posnett, The Mount, Higher Runcorn, where she was Professionalle engage 1. Deceased, who had been in at- tendance upon Mrs. Posnett for some days, complained of feeling ill en Friday. and ccnsulted Dr. Ormsby,who Prescribed for her. In the evening she took a dose of the medicine, remarking to Mrs. Posnett, " This is the Way'to take medicine.' Immediately afterwards she 'fell on the hedrocm floor and expired. Dr. Ormsby hal certified the cause of drath to be angina pectoris, and 013; Coroner has not deemed an inquiry necessary. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE 010 • WIDNES MAN. At the Dublin County Commission, before Mr. Justice 'O'Brien, on Thursday, a man named John Kelly, a native of Widnes, pleaded not guilty to an indictment Charging him with having on the 6th October attempted to commit suicide by cutting his throat with a razor. Mr. Herald Byrne, solicitor, pleaded guilty on his behalf. Edmond Kelly and Themas M'lnerney, brother and brother-in-law of the prisoner, went to Dublin to open a business in the coal trade. They failed, and that was the only reason that could be assigned for his rash act. The relatives promised to take him back to England if he were literated. His Lordship allowed the prisoner taut on his own recoenieances. OUR Imenovsantsv CLASSES. On Tursday, the Pickwick Clubtleeld its usual weekly Meeting when Mr. W. Millington continued his able Paper on "Errata.”—On Wednesday night at the S.M.I. Class, there was but a Mill attendance. Upon the "Question Box" being opened " Which is the greet,st Opponent of Christianity, drink or gambling ?" was brought to light. Oth^r questions nulled out of the box and spoken linen were "Why should we have an im- provement class ?" "What fascination is there about smoking ?" "Should we go to war with France ?" etc., •etc. Messrs. Saunders. Hayes,and W. Millington were aoaong the speakers. The Cuaii man for the evening was I. T. Simister.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRA.LLY. SIR J. T. BRUNNER OPENS THE NEW EXTENSION.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRA.LLY. SIR J. T. BRUNNER OPENS THE NEW EXTENSION.

APPRECIATION OF THE CHAD WICK BEQUEST. Sir J. T. Brunner, Bart., M.P., on Wednesdey afternoon, in the presence of a large aril influential gathering, formally opened the new Reading Room and extension ot the Runcorn Free Library. Of late years the library has been growing, and for some time its extension has.been a subject daily becoming more urgent. It will be remembered trot the late Mr. S. B. Chadwick of It uncora, bequeathed a valuable legacy of books and specimens of zoology. The acceptance of that gift made it imperative that the Library Committee should carry out an immediate extension. This was done and there have been added to the build- ing a vestibule entrance giving access to the building from Egerton-street, a ladies' reading- room. As the Library Committee were limited to a certain expenditure, their only source of income being a penny rate, they were compelled to econo- mise. Thus the improvements which have only cost something like £250, are on all hands con- sidered good value for money. The plans of the alterations were prepared by Mr. James Wilding (surveyor to the Council) and the whole work has been carried out under his personal supervision. By the re-arrangements the public and the librarian have increased facilities awl greater comforts. Bar- rower have better facilities for entering and leav- ing the building,which can be done without hinder ing the general reader. The carrying out of the arrangements reflects the highest credit upon , Mr. Wilding and it is Clear that no pains have been spared by him in the work.Mr.Chadwick's bequest was on view and open to the public for inspection for the first time. In addition to Sir John T. Brunner, Bart.,M.P.. there were also present at the opening ceremeny:—Mr Samuel Taylor (chairman of the Urban District Council), Messrs D Biabrown (Chairman of the Libraire Committee), M L Devlin, (Vice-chairman), W Hendley, W Hankinson, E Imison,Joseph Pritchard, T Riley,M J Sweetman, (mem- bers of the Library Committee), P Speakman, F J Nor- man, Dr McDougall, Dr Delaney,Messrs W Collier,James Pritchard, T Simister, J Wilson, G Bellamy, T Reynolds, D Jones, (librarian), J Lawrenson, J F Moulton, W Sutton, Rem H B Firth, G D Wray (Halton), C W L arid Christieo, S Wright, J A B Malvern It e odor,. • others. Mr. John Simpson sent a letter from Conway,' apologising for his abamce The proceedings opened with the members of the Library Committee, and other piablic bodies congregating in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall. At four o'clock they proceeded in procession to the new entranee In Raerton-street. Arrived there Mr.'S. Taylor (who wore his chain of offiee), in suitable terms presented Sir John Brunner with a silver key, and asked him On b half a the Library Committee to formally open the New Reading Room. Sir John Brunner said he accepted the key with which. se perform the ceremony with very great pleasure. Their meeting together that day was a memorial of a depleted citizen of very great worth (the late Mr. S. B. Chadwick. (Hear, hear.) Sir John having opened the door with his.preseatetion key, said he was very glad to epen that buinsine, as repeesentine the Library Com- mittee, and be declared it open and free to the public for all time. (Bear, hear.) The building was then entered and the company hav- ing inspected the extension and new-reading romn,a mast- jog was held over which Mr. S. Taylor presided. There were also on the platform in addition tie Sir John Brunner and Mr. Taylor, Mr. D Bisbrewn (chairman of the Library Committee), and Dr F McDoueall. The Chairman said he need not say that they were all delighted to have Sir John Brunner with them that day. They all knew that Sir John bad taken a very extensive interest in education for a number of years. Perhaps it would not be out of place if he (the speaker) was to say la few words in reference to the Library in the past. (Hear, hear). In 18d1, there was a requisition signed by a number of people and presented to Dr Steele (the then chairman of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners), requesting him to call a public meeting to entertain and otherwise consider the question of adopting the Lib- raries Act. That meeting was called, and there were he was pleased to remark, two persons now present who took a very active part in that meeting. He referred to Dr. Preston and Dr. McDougall. (Appla.ufre.) The tneetine, was addressed by those two gentlemen and by Mr. John Simpson and others. It was so put to that meeting, and by a large majority it was decided to adopt the Act and take a penny in the £ out of the rates for the purposes of the Library. In 1882 the Library was opened by Sir James Picton, in the old Board of Commissioner's Room, near the Police Station, where it was conducted for about 12 months. But it was found that the room was unsuitable, there was net sufficient accommodation so that the Board of Commission decided to remove their offices tothe present building, and they lent certain rooms for the Library. At the same time the public reading room was opened and it went on, he thought, anvil about 1885. It had been so suceessful, and bean made use of to such an ex- tent by the public of Runcorn, that it was considered they would have to make a move in providing better accommodation. They appealed to the Board of Corn. missioners and they gave them a little more accommo- dation. At the close of the first year of the work of the Library they had something likel,soo volumes. Thanks to Mr. John Simpson and others for their generosity in presenting the Library with a large number of books, the premises were again extended as years went by, but they soon became over- crowded again until last year they found them- selves in sucn a pnsition that they were compelled to make a move and do something. They had left to them by the late Mr. Chadwick about 2.000 volumes, and he might say that they had about 7,800 volumes of their own in round figures. They had therefore, at preieat,a, library of about 10,000 volumes (applause). Something had' te:be done, as they all knew, they had no power to tske more than a penny in the e ont of the rates, and they found that ways and means became a very serious obstacle. They were all aware that during the last few years the income of the library had not been what it was at one time—that was consequent on the depression of -the trade in the town. Still, notwithstanding those 1 difficulties standing in the way, as far as ways and! means went they found the question had to be faced. The result of their efforts was seen in the opening cere- mony. (Hear, hear.) He was sure they were all proud of their position that day—(applause)—and he hoped it would help them forward. At all events it was really aetonishing,as it was gratifying, to those who took such &deep intereat in the library, to find it made use of to the extent it was. (Loud applause.) • Sir John Brunner, on rising was warmly received. He said they knew that his acquaintance with Runcorn was now a very old one and a very long one. He made the acquaintance of 'Runcorn in 1881, and he had with thei Chairmanthe pleasure of watching the growth of Run- ecru not only in numbers but in some cases in beauty, and that which was nearer his heart its growth in public spirit. (Hear., hear.) When he first knew Runcorn the public spirit of the town was not shown in quite as marked a degree as it was that day. Be rejoiced with them in the change that had come over the people of the town. They were in the march with many another town of that dear land of theirs that they all loved so much, but they must not boast too much in saying that affairs were better with them than they were with their forefathers. Al! over the country from one end to the other, North to South, East to West, during their lifetime they had been closing prisons;; they had been opening schools, building libraries and open- ing hospitals. That was one of the victories of peace not less renowned than war. lThe hisiory of Runcorn and neighbourhood, he was able to say—and he was proud from his heart to say it—the history ef that constituency was a history of such meet- ings as that, and had been so for many a year. (Hear, hear.) When he was invited to come atd further the extension of the means of usefulness by opening the new rooms of the Public Library of Runcorn, he accepted the Incitation without theelightest hesitation and with very great pleasure. They were there, as he had already said, to render thanks and homage to the memory of Mr. Chadwick who 'had made them such a generous gift. Be (Sir John) was nothing if tee was not a practi- cal man, and he would ask if there was a catalogue of Mr. Chadwick's gift ?—Mr. J. D. Jones (librarian): Not yet; Sir John.—He would then beg of the Library Com- mittee that on every cno of those eases and below every one of these specimens there slowill be an inscription which would be a lesson in itself. (Hear, hear.) There was very little interest ii eyeing through a great museum or 'even a small museum if it was not wall catalegued, and .unless every object had an intelligible inecrintion mom it setting forth the name and habits of the animal, or describing it as the case might be. (Hear, hear). During the last two mouths on various occasions he had been—whilst in Seoland—surrounded by trophies of a similar character, and the only inscription that he found on any one of them was the date on which it was shot and the name of the man who shot it. KLaughter.) He recommended that each one of those specimens should be labelled so as to set forth all that was necessary in a concise way. A library, and the extension of a library such as that was an evidence to all men of a determination on the part of the public authority to be in line with the progress of c'vilisation, arid the tact that there were FO many of the leading men nf the town ps•eseat was a source of encouragement to the Library Committee,as well as to the Urban District Council. It showed that their work was appreciated by all. When they found the representative men nf a town gathered together as they saw them that day they would find their infinence would to throughout the whole population,and would elevate the people for whom they goverened. A library was everywhere regarded as an indispensable monunient of municipal civilization. He had read with very great interest the reports of the Library for many years,and though he did not mean for a moment to find fault, be would like to sec on those report.; a few words of erchorketiox with a view of tho
generous

div.head: EXAMINER FRP )A Y, OCTOBER 28, IS9B
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRP )A Y, OCTOBER 28, IS9B

direction of the public mind as to the reading to be un- dertaken. Year by year their thoughts travelled in different directions, and there was in the main a new Stream of thought every year going in a particular vein. Now an intelligent man stow rintending a library would do his duty towards the public if every year he mentioned some book relating to the subject with which the public mind was for the time filled. When in the city of Toronto, the Creel Librarian of that very progressive cite told him that the Library Court completed a turn of the screw every year that the Library was in existence, so raising its io- tellectual tone. Heremembered very well coming home to tell the story that at Toronto he heard teat ev.we year there were lectures given by competent men with rezard to the contents of the library in its different de- partments. Teey knew that every year they had it from his own lips,and tiny knew with what pleasure he heard that Runcorn had determined to foPow in that direction and to have those IPetUreEl. His only point WAS he wanted the Library C enmittee to take credit to ilself for the work it did,and to put a few words in the annual report with regard to its work. Another thought th it always recurred t) his mind when thinking about a lib- rary was that two men sitting in a linrary were for the moment on an absolute equality. Two men reading Shakespeare, two men reading Milton, two men read tog any Philos mher were for the num:int on an equality. They were in the society and intrrcourse of tne hest of mankind, and it was an equality which they could practice without any loss for the m oment of faith. It was an equality which all could aim at. An equality of the material condition was the dream of the wild socaliat, but this equality of mental altenmeneequality of spiritual condition was attainable only by intercourse with the best minds that God had seat down on earth. (Hear, hear and applause.) That comic] be had from that Library. (Applause.) He had called it a victory of peace rand he had expressed the hope that ceremonies of that kind might be just as frequent in the future as they had been in the past. But they were living in times when it was impossible that a man who had any sense of public duty upon his miod, to address his fellowmen without a word about those ter iOll3 responsi- bilities that were resting daily upon them. They were living amidst rumours of war —espeeially rumours about a war that would be a disaster to the whole world, and tee civilisation. They were living in fear of war with their nearest neighbour, and he hoped it was the duty of all of them,of every man amongst them ,to face their responsibility. (Hear, hear.) They were I abeut, or they might be ab out t) quarrel with France about a part of the world of which none of teem knew very much. It was a part Jf the world which was very [little worth quarrelling about It was a country the climate of which was impossiLle for Europeans. They could no live in it or bring uo their families there. The neighbouring district went by the name of the Congo free state and was in the possession of the King of the Belgians. His Majesty boasted some time ago of the I great sacrifices which had been made by the Belgians in the artquisitien and defence of the territory. The average life of the officers who had gone to the Congo was five months. They knew by the newspapers that during the last few menthe England had lost neatly more lives through enteric fever than were lost toy fire arms or !sword in Egypt. It was a country that was about RS little worth anything as any country in the world. There was another consideration that in Africa they had got into an extremely unwhole annoy metherd of colonization. Colonies were not for the community in Afri3a. They were for the benefit of men who got up Companies; in London. (Hear, hear.) He would be very sorry if the great sienna) that they had In Egypt were to result in the formation of a Chartered Company. On the other hand they had given way in a Christian spirit, he believed, to many a demand made by France for the last ten years. It might be righte- ously said—he did not know—that they had given way eneuehond on this occasion they could not give way. But If they did go into the fight they should remember that it was not for the acquisition of territory, not for the increase of their wealth, but on the sole ground of the , defence of their honour. (Applause.) Mr. Taylor hid told him that the Library Committee had been limited 'in their work by the funds at their disposal. They had spent upwards of £250 on that building, whereas they would have liked to spend rather more than twice that amount, something like £6OO. But that would have made such a hole in the proceeds of the penny rate that there would have been very little money to spend for books. In another town in Cheshire he had sen that the library was supplemented by an extremely pleasant means. A book society had teem formed which bought books, circulated them amongst the memb°rs, and at the end of twelve months they made them a present to the library. This was done in return for the , eervices of the librarian as hen. seer .tary to the society. Re hoped that somebody would start a book society in Runcorn with the SAMS organization and the same happy reselt.He was rather afraid that he would be looked upon as; finding a good deal of fault that day if he said that the lie of subscriptions; to the library—which ought to ek3 out the Id in the 2—was n t a long one, for that reason he made the suggestion about a book society. He again assnred them of the very great pleasure with which he had joined them in the ceremony that day. He had had peculiar pleasure in it because as he had said it com- memorated a very kindly hearted and public spirited rnan and because it was another event in the now long history of Runcorn. (Hear, heir, and applause.) Mr. D. Risbrown said he Was certain that every one in that room would express the feelings of the Library Committee and the Urban District C ouncil and their own in the pleasure they felt at having Sir John Brunner amongst them. He rose to move a resolution ; and having at leneth given a resume of the work of the library committee he concluded by proposing" That the best thanks of this meeting be given to Sir J. T. Brunner, Bart., M.P., f r opening the reading room,and for the admirable address he has jubt delivered." (Applause.) Mr. M. L. Davies seconded the motion with !pleasure. As one who had scene intimate knowledge of the work of the Library Committee, he felt that the presence of Sir John Brunner amongst them was due to the very great interest he always evinced in things appertaining to Runcorn, and especially the library. (Applause), Dr. McDougall said he need hardly tell them how much pleasure it gave him to supoort the vote. He dealt at length with the formation of the library. It was 30 years since first he came to Ittancorn,and at that time educational matters were not so progressive as in the present day. He spoke of the late Mr. Chadwick Who was a man who did a lame amount of good work, but never at any time did he let his right hand know what his left was doing: (Hear' hear-) He trusted that Sir John would be long spared to continue his deep interest I in thoile matters: (Loud applause): The Chairman intimated that a telegram had just been handed in from Mr. Mather,(chairman of the Cast-1 tier Kellner Campany), stating that he was unable to be present. It was a circumstance they all regretted. Mr. W. Handley further supported the resolution. He could go a little further hack that Dr. McDougall,whem ' he remembered coming to cho town. In those times it was said of Runcorn" There was one way in and no way nut." (Langbter).But since then things had altered. The library committee would continue to do ita work and would not rest until they had established a museum for Runcorn. (Loud applause.) • The vote was put from the chair, and carried with acclamation. Sir John Brunner in acknowledging said that in the futnrea he would try and do something to deserve all the geed things that had been said about him. div.p: FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS.
DEATH OF A RUNCORN MAN.

On Wednesday morning, Mr. J E. Worley. held an inqurst at the Police St—tion. Runlorn, touching the death of Mr. Charles Mounfield. aged 70 Tars, who was found dead in his house in Balfour-street on Monday night.

_ _ Sarah Tittle,vrife of William Tittle, Balfour-stree,,Run- corn, said on Monday she saw deccmed, who was her father. He had been dohs. a little whitewashing and complained to her af bring stiff and suffering from what 'he called cramp. She hnrself aVributed it to the exer- tion of whitewashing. Later on in the day shefelt anxi- ous about him and went up to the house but could not get in. After roaming about for some rim, she went home and had supper. About eleven o'clock she again went to her father's house,iti company with hr husband and they effected an ertrance with some here. They could not find deceased anywhere about the kitchen,but on searching the cellar her husband found him at the bottom of the stairs apparently dead. William Tittle, husband of the foregoing witness, con roloorated. adding that he found the deceased face down- I wards. its one hand he had hold of a coal scuttie and in the other was a shovel. He was of opinion that his father-in-law had been fetching coal and when in the act of returning fell backwards downstairs. Dr. McLennan was sent for and pronounced life extinct. Police Constable Gregory gave similar evidonc.. There was a wound at the back of deceased's head three inches long and two slight ones on the forehead. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death.'

He went inside and demanded the return of the money whereupon the landlord got hold of him by the throat alai tried to chuck him out. div.head: RUNCORN VOLIJTEEI PRIZi DISTRIBUTION.
div.p: RUNCORN VOLIJTEEI PRIZi DISTRIBUTION.
GRAND CONCERT.

PRESENTATION OF PRIZES BY LADY BROOKE. Tuesday evening, the evening upon which the Rencorn Volunteers received the prizes they had won in connection with the annual camp and shooting meeting, from the hands of Lady Brooke, will long live in the memory of Runcorn peeple as a night which afferded to them one of the finest musical treats ever heard in the town. Through the strenuous exertions of their popular commander— (Captain George Ashton)—the services of the world renowned Rhondda Royal Male Choir,and a number I of talented artistes, including Madame Williams- Penn (soprano), Miss Bessie Jones (harpist), Miss Mabel Teasley (violinist), were engaged, with the gratifying result stated above. An additional at- traction was provided by the Runcorn Volunteer Band which contributed two capitally performed pieces. The audience was extremely large and fashionable and include 1 all the elete of Runcorn and district. The Hall was tastefully decorate I. The Volunteer Band opened with a selection from Iffeyerbeer's works, but its effect was greatly lost through the noise occasioned in the hall whilst the audience were becoming seated. The Rhondda Glee Society followed with "Comrades in Arms " (Adams), and were heartily encored giving " Fare- well my own true love." Miss Bessie Jones proved an accomplished harpist,end both her contributions " Welsh Melodies" and "Dense de Sylphs " were well executed. Miss Mabel Tan-ley's violin solos, ware a pleasing performance. Slats gave "Sessendef ( Wianowski), and the same composer's "2nd Mazourka." The latter rendition was a marvel of musicianly execution. Mr. David Jones at once established a popularity for himself wite his solos ' "Blow, Blow" and " Queen of the Earth," both of which were encored. " Eos Dar " (good nightin- Rile) the popular pennillion singer diverted the audience with some excellent specimens of his home spun poetry. Madame Williams-Penn, a soprano of fine compass, was always a favourite. Her singing of" The Swallows " and " For all eternity " dis- played her voice to advantage. She Yeas de- servedly encored. In the duet " sol-fa " (by request) Madame Williams-Penn and Mr. Dated Jones provided a refined exhibition of vocal culture. The items rendered by the Choir included 'The Tyrol " (Arnbroise Thomas), "The Pilgrims" (Parry), "The Soldier Chorus" (Gounod) "Day and Night" (Alfrel Dard), "Italian Salad" (Genee), and with the several encores, were per- fect' The most appreciated perhaps was the " Soldiers Chorus." The Volunteer Band in the opening of the second part gave 'A Selection from Mendellsohn" (C. Godfrey), and were highly ap- plauded for an interesting performance. During the interval the presentation of p-izes was made by Lady Brooke, who Was supported on the platform by the Rev. Dr. Preston (chaplain of the Battalion), Captain George Ashton (F. and G. Companies, 2nd V.B. Cheshire), Captain Thomas, Captain ivans, Major Harrisen,Lieutenant Morrice, Lieutenant Bromley, Rev. H. B Illoate (chaplain.) In introducing Lady Brooke, Captain Ashton said before calling upen her Ladyship to make the pre- sentation, it woold be his duty to give an account or the condtart of the Runcorn Volunteer.. On the whole, he had a very good report to submit, the attendances at drill were better than ever. Since last year the shooting had impr3vel wo Modally ; whilst last year the averaee per man was 76 points, this year it reached 93 pointe per man. They would be pleased to see that this year the best shot in the whole Battalion belonged to Rule nei. (Ap- plause). Ths Battalion cup tied been won by Sereeant Edwards (applaese), and it had been won in such a war that would be remembered by the Rene:ern Detneement for all time. Sergeant Eivenrd's won the cup with a tot 1 0170 pints, out of a po.sible 70 (renewed applause). Si that every shot was a " hull's eve " (increased applause). Th.? prize for tea smartest man in the battalion was also wen by • Rencern. (Applause).—Captain Ashten eeeleined at this point that there would also be pa 841'sd that night three long-service melnle and also the cup given by Sir Richard te-noke. Part., which should have been presentel on previeue occasion. The recipients of the long service medals would be Colour-Sergeant W. H. Hersey. Sergeant J. A. Reeliton, aed Corporal G. ' Shingle?. CANON CRAIG ON THE DOCTRINE OF TRANSUBSTANTIATION.

On Sunday last, the annual sermons were preached at St. Edward's Catholic Church, Runcorn, moraine and evenine, on behalf of the Day schools held in coauection with the Mission. The preacher was the Very Rev. Canon Craig, of Crewe. Both services were well-attended I and the eloquent discourses were listened to with devout I attention. In the morning Canoe Craig founded his sermon on the words " I shall be your God ; and you shalt be my p-ople; and I shall walk in your midet,saith the Lord of iilStS." Those words meant that it was clearly God's intention to be always with them—present at every Catholic Ceurch, in the sacred Increment of the Altar. He was their Gad; they were His people, and He walked in their midst. They accepted it in its literal sense. They believed it. Thera must have been some- thing charming in the human race that God should promise to be ever with them. God had never made any promise to be ever with the angels, but He made that distinction for men. In the 6th chapter of St. John's Gospel, there was a passage in which our Lord stated "I am the living Breal which came down from Heaven ; if any man eat of tills Bread he shall live forever,etc."That Wag a promise th at Our Blessed Lord fulfillel at that last supper before His death. He took bread which He brake saying "This is my body,eat this," and taking th wine "This is my blood, drink this." It was per- fectly clear that our Lord meant that it should be taken in its literal meaning. Tne preacher dealt with the con- tention welch was so often put forward by the opponents of their religion, and br the a iherents of the so called Reformation, that in the Syrio-Cnaldaic language there was no word—no verb that could have been wee by our Lord which would have conveyed the equivalent of represents." They contended that our Lord meant "Ties " represente' mv nody." "Tots " represents" my blood," but that ceni:entioo tell to the ground because there ware something like 400 worde in the Syria c ,eithee haneu lee t sat woit'd have stood as tha eqdiva - lent of represents. In the evening the rev, preacher continued his address on Transubstantiation. It was a doctrine they hid ever s:t forth, and wood continue to set filth. Torougo the hlisf in test doc- trine they looked upon their Churches as a Heaven upon earth. Ii the Tabernacle upon the Altar they had in the person of the Host—the DiVio9 Second Person of the Helv Trinity. And as the Second Person of the Trinity was presanc,Goil film iell was present,and • so was the Weisel Holy Spirit, for where one was there were also the otbcr two. Canon Craig emcluded his ra. marks with an exhortation to his hearers 1 to be self- sacrificing in the response to the appeals of their past= (the Rev. H. B. Gore) who was appealing to theta OR behalf of the 17,,,ry exlellent Schools that were connected with the Mission, and whose good work was so hi,hly commendable.—The altar bad been tastefully decorated with choice chrysanthemums and maidenhair ferns by Miss B. Gore. The music was Farmer's Mass is B flat. The organ was efficiently presided over by Mrs. Stan- cliffe, Regent-street, and the musical portion of the ser vice throughout reflected creditably upon the abilities ef Mr. Hackney (the choirmaster and conductor).

Not a single note of disapproval has so far been raised ‘r,ainst the selection of Mr. Joan Morley to vvrite` no authorised biography of Mr. Gladstone. Mr Morley was marked out for the work from the °merit of the stateman's death—if, indeed, he had not already undertaken some preliminary labours in connection with it during Mr. Glaistone's life- time, and with Mr. Gladstone's assistance. His frequent visits to Hawarden after the Liberal leader's retirement were generally supposed to have some bearing on the biographical work which the public are now promised from his pen, and his long absences from Parliament this year were attributed to the same cause. I think it may be taken for granted that Mr. Morley's new task will have the effect of withdrawing his energies for a time from the field of current political controversy. Now that the Home Rule movement is a state of suspended animation, there is no question before the country in which his mini is very greatly absorbad.Prequent as were his absences from the House of Commons last session, they are likely to be even more pro- longed during the remaining term of this Parlia- ment's existence.

Reference has been made by one of the Vienna plague doctors to the case of three sailors in a ship in a London dock who were found to be infected with the disease two years ego, and who were treated in one of the hospitals. A well-known London bacteriologist informs me that this occur- rence of plague in London was in the winter of 1896, and was kept a profound secret, in order to prevent anything like a panic. My informant also recalled the fact that in the present year a passen- ger steamer from Bombay had to put plague pa- tients ashore, firet at Malta and then at 6outhamp- ton, and that at b3th places the infection was suc- cessfully stamped out. The conditions of research in Europe are, however, almost certain to be made more strict. The question as regards this country will be raised the moment Parliament meets. Path- ological laboratories, it is felt, may be an even greater danger than powder magazines, and ought to be removed to places remote from populous cen- tres.

The Sirdar's grave description of the welcome ex- tended to him at Fashoda by the man in proces- sion has excited some more or less sar lonical mirth There is really a suggestion of opera boufle in Major Marchand's stately message to the victorious Sirdar apprising him that he has taken note of his inten- tion to come to Fa-hoda. " Where I shall be bappk to welcome you in the name of France." Lord Kit- chener. while paying a handsome compliment to the courage, devotion, aria indomitable spirit dis- played by the Marchand Expedition, allows the facts as to the nature of the gallant major's Occupa- tion to speak for themselves. These supplemen- tary despatches, indeed, make it clearer than ever that the tiny force was on the verge of annihilation when it was saved by the battle of Omdurtnanond also that Major Marchand and his companions are to this moment dependent for the mein of exist- ence on the bounty of their English rivals. Truly. as 1.40 rd Kitchener remark., their position would be ludicrous had not their sufferings an I privations rendered it pathetic. A novel musical recital, of which the novelty proved to be quite an incidental attraction, was Riven at the St. James's Hall on Monday afternoon by Messrs. Ross and Moore, " Ensemble Fianists,". who made their debut at the Berlin Philharmonic Concerts a few years ago, and have glace toured through Europe. Their unison ia .almost magically perfect. Seated, at opposite sides of the platform there is as complete an understanding between them as though, they were together before the same pianoforte. They make the two pianos seem like one glorified. Their programme this afternoon was exceptionally varied, and must have involved a severe strain on the memory, for the two artistes play without book. Nevertheless the precision and mutual sympathy which characterise their interpre- tations did not once fail them.

It would be a bit of amusing irony if it should fall to a British court of justice to lift the veil from the mystery which hangs over the Dreyfus case,yet that is a possible consequence of the action which Major Esterhazy is bringing against the "Observer." As both parties are prepared to fight their differences out to the end, and as they have placed their interests in the hands of the most com- petent solicitors of the day, the action may develop consequences of the most far-reaching character. Evidence from France either for the One. party or the other may not be forthcoming to an extent sufficient to uaravel the tangled skein of the Drey- fus mystery; but the questions which will be raised and such evidence as may be forthcoming will go a long way to remove the veil from the history of this transaction. Major Esterhazy In the witness - box will have his story to tell, and the contributor to the " Observer," who professed to intimate a knowledge of the transacrious which have been occurring in Franca,will have to make good his aszertions, if iome of his conclusions are not,mere hasty and immature inferences of his own; drawn from facts within his knowledge. But I fear there is nr.t much likelihood of the case being ripe for hearing soon.

div.p: GENERA 1 NEWS.

Dr. IV ueller. who was attacked by plague after the death of the hospital attendmt Bartsch. at Venice died on Monday. Successful experiments have been ma-le in the south- 'western district of Queens'and in the destruction of rabbits by infecting them with chicken cholera. Another Attempt at train.wreeking, believed to be the work of boys, has been discovered on the Midland line between Kettering and Desborough. Damage estimated at £20.000 was caused by fire on Wednes- day morning at Cameron Bridge Distillery, near Leven. Five hundred barrels ofwhiskv were pestroyed. . . .

According to the Kreuz Zeltung, It has been decided to despatch into the Oameroons hinterland a numerous and well equipped German expedition, which will penetrate as far as Lake Tchad. The roof of a church In the Faubourg de Santr Lucia. Verona. which WAS undergoing repairs, fell in on Senday morning. The Ref.tident was'attended by serious consequences several lives being lost.

News has been received at Memel that the barque Satisfac- tion, of this port,Capt +ln Hord], from Leith for Memel with coal, has sunk In the North Sea. The captain, his wife, and nine of the crew perished, a boy alone being saved by a Gothenburg steamer. From Shanghai It is reported that, within a period of eigh- teen days, six fires, all of a serious character, have occurred at Hankow. Thousands of lives have been lost, and much valuable property destroyed. The tires are supposed to be the work of Incendiaries. _

Fourteen of tte crew of the British steamer Astrea, sunk in the Gulf of Lyons after collision with a French steamer. were landed at Plymouth on Monday. They assert that while on the French steamer they had to sleep on the deck, without shelter of any kind. At Chester on Saturday. a guard named Thomas David Thomas was committed to the assizes for trial on Charges 0' stealin7 articles while in transit, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company. It was stated that the total amount of the robberies represented a value of about £l4O. Rioting has occurred at San Salvatore, near Allessandria. Piedmont. Italy, In consequence of the measures taken by th e local authorities to extirpate phylloxera. Troops had to be sent to the district, and the soldiers were compelled to use their rifles, with the result that four peasants were killed and I over twenty wounded. An extraordinary scene was witnessed at Chatham on Sunday night, when a crowd of young men wrecked a house lin New-road, declaring it to be haunted. The windows werel smashed, a,bl the doors covered with mud, but the appear- ance of a strong force of police prevented further destruction. The house is furnished bot untenanted. At Cardiff on Saturday, a woman named Slade was shot, it la supposed, by her reputed husband, who subsequently, committed suicide. A man named Mott. sixty yearn of age was brought before ham magistrates on Saturday in connection with the death of his wife, who died, according to the report, from injuries inflicted by hini. James Merton, aged thirty-nine, a bricklayer s labourer. of 44, Leigh-Ms& Hindley Green ebrunsitted" subide on Friday by cutting his throat with a razor., He ,as employeel at the erection of a local church. On Friday he complained ti his landlady of being unwell. arra asked ter his razor.' He said he was about to sell it; he went back to his work, and was found with a fatal gash in his throat. _

_ Mr. Thomas O'Dwyer Russell, stated to be a folly-qualified physician and residing In Manchester, is in custody of the London police on a charge of breaking a window in the office of "Punch." Fleet-str,.et. He states that he struck at the cartoon in th, window—which represents Marchaod as a " monkey up a stick "—because be thought it was a shame that Frenchmen should be compared to monkeys. The !dent ty of the young man who shot himself in a rail- way carriage between London and Broxbourne on Thursday has been established. Ile was Kenneth Napier Sergeant. twenty-one years of age, son of Mr. Albert sergeant, solicitor, of Hackney. At the inquest at Broxbourne. the father said his son was studying for his final examination, and the con- sequent overwori probably uahinged his mind. A verdict to that effect was returned.

The town of Hirpe—r;Sille. ten miles from Forest, Meals- sipt. is the eceneof a race war which, beginning on Saturdar night, bed up to ten o'clock on Sunday night resulted in MI death Of ten negroes ant one white, and the wounding of three whites and a number of negroes. The fight originated In the attempt of a constable and a posse of fifteen to arrest a man named Burke, a negro desperado, for the attempted murder of a white man. At Birkenhead on Saturday. Esther Gregg, aged about sixty, was charged on her own confession with the wilful murder of her son, Henry Bdward Grecg, in the year 1858. The woman had made a statement at the pollee station that she had found the deceased wading at Tranmere beach, and pushed him into the water. The bench, being of opinion that the prisoner is of unsound mind, remanded her for a fortnight to the lunatic ward of the workhouse hospital.

div.head: ketters to the Mttor. THE MAGISTRATES AND THE LIQUOR TRAFFIC.
div.p: ketters to the Mttor. THE MAGISTRATES AND THE LIQUOR TRAFFIC.

Sir,—Many and sore are the evils which betel a p"ople where class legislation prevails. It was this legislation which deprived the masses of our cDuatrynton of their just inheritance in the land, and the same legislation set seer and maintains the liver traffic. Yes,the British Par- hameet, which is supposed to represent the high at cul- ture and the greatest wisdom of this Christian country, deems it a pert of its duty te legalise the open manufac- ture and sale of liquids echos) use blights the physical, moral, and social conditions of the people to an extent almost incredible. And then we have another class of men who, althouell moving on a lower platform, are not babied our legislators in pushing the sale of drink. These are " the great unpaid," the men who are elevated to the "Bence', in some cases at least, mere as a reward for political services than for any pecu'iar fitness for magisterial fun- ctions. To these magistratee Parliament delegates the power of licensing but, t the crsdit of Parliament it must be said that power is not compulsory. The magis- trates may grant or refuse licenses at their own discre• ties. Bearing this in mind I have watched the action of the megistrat re at the reeent Brewster Sessions over a wide field with the result that I am more than ever con- vince that "The grest unpaid " are even more responsible than the legislature for the disorder, crime, and misery produced by drink. With a few honourable exceptlons,here and there,the justices showed themselves to be heart and soul with the publicans, licensing right and left, with a total disvgerd for any interests but those of the applicants. efortunately for the peace and welfare of Warring- ton, our Brewster Sessions on the 25th of August did not prove to be one or three tanneurabl a exceptions to the general swim in favour of the dealers in drink. It some- times happens at our court that cases have to wait for the presence of a magistrate ; but on the occasien re- ferred to, there was an abundant supply, no less than fifteen being present. And as these were all local men, well acquainted with the sins and so.rows of Warring- ton throuzh drink, one might have reasonably hoped that their flocking together ces the occasion was to d something to retrieve the stigma of drunkenness which has so long been associated with the t owe. But alas, for human expectations. The manner in which the Justices treated the appeals that were made to them on behalf of poor humanity had ea sinister look, aid it soon le apparent that their 'one, and only object, on the bench that day, was to play into the han is of the Brewers. Ani that object they carried out by granting further facilities for spreading tempt ttions in the way of the working classes. Bit why was this discreditable, this deploreble policy pursued? There was nothing in the police report pre- lented to the meeistrates te warrant it. That rsport stated the estimated population of the borough to be 62,000, with a licensed house for every 293 of the inha- bitants. But all the people are not consumers of liquor. rutting infants, children of tender age, young persons net yet contaminated by drink, wornee, and abstainers torther I think I may hezerd the assmption that they represent about five-sixths of the whole community, leaving the other sixth, or say 10,333 as the publicaa's clients!. And dividing the latter figures by 211,the RUM- b.r o' licensed houses in the borough, I arrive at the astouneing coaclusion that Warriogtoe has a driek seep estebliehed by law for every 49 of the inhabitants who prefer alcoholic lvverages ! There was, however, an item in the r &ice statisties which seemed to favour the magistrates' policy. Only 278 persons, or an average of one and a half for each public house, had been proceeded against for drunken- ness daring the year. But it must be borne in mini that these were extreme cases, anoetly pem men wh were rendered outrageous and combative by the liquids they had swallowed, and had, of course, to be punished by the magistrates for their bad behaviour. But will any sensible person believe for a moment that the polies owe represent anything hut the smallest friction of the drunkenness which prevails amongst us? Toe condition of the crow Is that are turned out of the pub'ic-houses every night in the week, especially on Saterdays and Sunday', gives one a very poor opinion of the sobriety e of the town. lier was it ignorance of the effects el drink that led the magistrates to be so liberal with the publicans. They knew what a feeder " the trade" was to the work- house, the asylum, and the jail ; they knew that while they were comfortably seated on their bench mel.ituies of their fellow townsmen were drageing net a miserable existence in nakednese and hunger through drink ; and they knew also that in times of t a(le depression the cheap philanthropy of the soup kitchen had to be re- sorted to in order to save some of the weer victims of intemperance from actual starvation. But these things moved them not ; they were not their brothers' k I have sometimes heard and read that bribery and corruption are net altogether strangers in some exalted places in the land; but perish the thought that such 'Seines could be found in Werrington ! Brutus who stahbed Ce Isar was an honourable man, and our maeistrates are all men of the same stamp eltenueh they dealt a severe blew to the best interests of the town. In Warrington, at any rate, I f •el sure that brewers'eold and beewere'patrooage could not blind the eyes of the judges. In old times it was said that whem the gods wished to deetrey they first deprived of sight. Has it come to this that Bacchus has ao distorted the vision of our legislet.ers and maeistraees that they can- not see that the liquor traffie is rapidly driving the nation to destrustien. This is really the only theca.7 that rill account for the marvellous spread and pros- perity of" the trade" in all directions. And is it not a sign, too, that a retributive providence is using the traffic to punish ue f or the d-barement and drunkenness we have for ages inflicted upon many Pf the poor and ignorant peoples of the world. Yours truly, lONA.

div.head: Bo Y BITTEN BY A DOG.
div.p: A Bo Y BITTEN BY A DOG.

On We Inesday nighr, Nlatthew Smith, 17 years of age, living at 90, Athol-street, Earlestown, was bitten by a dog in Clarence-street. The dog, which was without a muzzle, was lying in the middle of the fo)toath. He asked the owner to call the dog away whilst he parsed, but instead of doing so, the owner gave the dog a kick and said "fetch him." The dog thereupon ran at the yenta and bit him on the hand, and the wound had to be dressed by a medical man. The mutter was reportel to the police. WAnGRAvE CHURCH ("nom _ . .

On FridaY.;;;Ering—a -r—ocial gathering of this choir and several friends took place in the War. grave schoal. There were 52 present. and dancing whic'a commenced at 8 o'clock, was kept up with spirit until midnight. During the intervals, songs were given by the following, Miss Gorse, Miss Gaff, Messrs. W. and R. Carson, S. Dring, Liptrott, Ap- pleton, Shaw, and Wagg. Mr. A. Walker presided at the piano. and a mast enjoyable evening was spent. P.S.A. .

_ On Sunday af ternocn the ordinary meeting of the P S.A. was given up to the Rope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Temolars in c3nnectioa with their 26-,h anniversary. Taere was a large attendance and the gathering was presided over try the Rev. C. H. Murray of Manchester. The principal speaker was the Rev. J. H Doddrell of Prescot, all the addresses being chiefly upon Temperance matters. Vocal selections were given by Mrs. Williams and Mr. J. Webster, and Mr. W. Willis, presided at the piano. SHOCKING FATALITY TO A SLATER. On Monday morning John O'Neill, a slater of 15, Back Duke-street, Earlestown, met with his death by falling from the roof of a house in Haydock-st. The deceased, who was well known in the district, was an efficient man at his business, and had slated the roofs of almost all the houses in Earlestown.He was stated to be 54 y ears of age. He was living apart from his wife, and on Mon lay morning about 9 o'clock went to the house of his daughter, 23, Lawrence-street, Earlestown, with whom his wife was living. He left again at 930, saying he was going to work. His wife pressed him not to go, as she thought he had been drinking. Ho was engaged repairing the roof of a house in Raydock-street,he- longing to Bailey Brothers, and be was found at 10.45 lying at the foot of a ladder by Harry Richards. of 82, Haydock-street, and he was then dead. His skull and left leg were fractured. Dr. Valentine who was called to deceased expressed the opinion that death was due to concussion of the brain.—The inauest was held on Tuesday afternoon at the Railway Hotel by Mr.Brighouse and evidence bearing out the above facts was given. Nobody saw the deceased fall, and a verdict of " Accidental death" was returned.

On Monday evening the Earlestown District School (Infants' department) was crowded to excess, on the occasion of an entertainment by the scholars of the infant selsool, of which Mrs. Brown is head- mistress. A large temporary platform was erected at one end of the room by Mr. G. Finning, and a large curtain was drawn across. For some time past the children have been undergoing special training at the hands of Mrs. Brown, who had the able assistance of the other teachers including Misses King, Banks, Hughes, Tripp and Haynes. Unfortunately, however, Mrs. Brown was taken ill a few days prior to the entertainment, and was un- able to be present on Monday night. Still the children had been so thoroughly trained and the assistant teachers were so well up in their work that the absence of Mrs. Brown was no drawback to the success of the entertainment. Miss Hughes presi led at the piano,and aceomplished her arduous task in a very efficient manner. The programme included the usual items of action songs and choruse,, but several of the pieces deserve special mention. The May Pole song and dance by 12 little girls was an admirable production, and the music emanating from the Kazoo band of 18 boys was most amusinz. The drill by 32 boys ts soldiers was capitally executed. and the duet "Where are you going to ?" by Eva Davies and Fred Finall was so excellently executed that the aulience demended a recall. The dance " Lancers" by 8 couples was capitally gone through and they had to repeat one or two of the figures. The recitation "So tired 'by May Hill, Eva Eltion an IL. Dilworth, was very well given and heartily applauded. All the other items were given with equal success. and at the close a vote of thanks was moved by the Rev. T. R. Matthews, and seconded by Mr. A. Peake. Mr. Brown",responded on behalf of !kin. Brown. The ;concert was continued on Tuesday night, wheß the room .was again well filled

Since i:s introduction to the public Dr. Tibbles' Vi-Cocoa has met with phenomenal success and gained a popu- larity hitherto nokanwn in the trade. A representative of this paper has made an insoection of the window displays of Dr. Tibbles' Vi-Cocoa in Warrington and district and iet r viewed the purvevers and vendors respecting its sales and progress. Everywhere the verdict was the same ' • the demand for Dr. Tibbles' Vi-Cocoa is increasing and the sale is far and away ahead of all competitors. It is almost unnecessary to enter into any description of the Vi-Cocoa itself. Its merits are well-known and greatly appreciated. The qualities of Vi-Cocoa are many and have been testified to over and over again by all sorts and conditions of mew It posses +es wonderful recuperative powers and has proved of benefit to both brain ,vorkere and the " horny-haaded sons of toil." No secret is made by the proprietors as to its properties. It consists of cocoa, kola, malt and hope, all of which are substances of marvellous dietetic value. This food beverage has the refreshing properties of fine tea, the nourishment of the best ccoae, and a tonic and recupera- tive force possessed by neither. It can always be used in cases where tea and coffee are prohibited. To tho'e who htye lost their appetites Vi-Cocoa works wonders. In short it has been found to lighten fatigue, remove depression and relieve mental strain and worry •, it strengthens digestion, and is a perfect beverage for children and invalids and all who are subjected to physical and mental exertion. The demand for it in the district may be gauged by the experience of local trades- men as related to the reporter. Messrs. Henry Milling and Company. Limited, florsemarket-etreet, devoted one window exclusively to a display of Dr. Tibhlee' Vi-Cocoa.
