EARLESTOWN.

The annivergary dinner and meeting irt nonnectioo with the Loyal Viaduct Lodge, No. 2686 Manchester Unity of 0 idfellows was held at the Wellington Hotel, Earlestown on Saturday evening. There were 61 mem- . bers and vieitors to dianer which was excellently served by P.G. J. W. Thorpe, and thoroughly enjoyed. After dinner the cloth was removed, and the subsequent pro*. ceedings were presided over by N.G. Bro, James Seddon, the vice chair being oscupied by Bro. W. Sutton P.P.G.M. A letter of apology for non-attendance aVati read fr am Brother Brockhank, St. Helens. After the usual loyal toast had been proposed and htmourecl, Rem. Teomas Tunstall, P.P.G.M., proposed the toast of the Manchester Unity and Roan i of Directors" aad in I doing so said it was a society of which there wss no I equal. It was organised for the purpose of enabling in'n wbo had a little thought about themselves for making provision in case of sicaness, and leaving 3 deceit funeral. The rate of contribution in that Sonistv " small, and there was no ether society that could give the same amount of contribution. It was a society the assisted, as far as it could, the distressed brethren in the lodge when called upon. (Hear, hear.) The rate of con- tribution in support of distressed members only amounted to about one penny per member per annum. He did not say that the Society was perfect, bet could be improved, and they could much reduce the rate of contribution, so that such a thing as eistress would never be known. (Applause.) He would like to see the A.M.C. bring forward something which would make the society a charitable one, as well as a benefit society, in order to assist those distressed who deserved it. The Board of Directors were men from the ranks and they cou'd he depended upon to see that the society was managed on an economical basis. The toast was honoured in true Oddfellow fashion. Bro. W. Mawdsley sang "Good oil Jeff,* Bro. W. Sephton gave "Queen of the Earth," and Bro. W.Sutton, P.P.G.M., recited " Heart's Charity." Bro. John Tonstall, P.P G M , o' Liveipool,remonding to the toast of " The Manchester Unity," said that w is the 27th occasion on which he had been pres ins. He looked forward to the invitation to attend that ga hering with the greatest amount of pleasure. He recolleoted P.G.M. E. Smith being rresent at one of their meetiny,s at a most entioal time in their history when he gays them words of wisdom which were long remembered by P.P.G.M. Hughes, Wright,Brockbank, and other, had Cools there to enjoy themselvea,and at the name time to give thorn the benefit of their opinions to the best ef their ability, and to adviee them the right course to adopt in connection with the society. Th. Oldfollo yes Socisty. stortsd in a very humble way about the year 1810, and for years was yillified and scandal- ised by s erne of the highest in the land ; clergymen, and men in all profsesione had not a kind woe,' to say about. the M.U., or Friendly Societys generally. The^ lookei upon them as co many traitors, aid pisttera against the S:ate, going to ups it the Houses of Parliament. But what a change had come over the snirit of the dream. He was happy to say that three-fourths of the members of the House of Commons were membere of this society. Bishops had thoushr it an honour to become ini•iatod in tie Order;Pe-rs rif tho realm hal only ben too delightes to take a part in the affairs of the aneiety;and they fe coed at the present time the richest and strongest Friendly Society in the world. (Hear, hear ) They had 925,110 members. There were other societies working in the same eroove as they were, almost on the same liees.and doing their share of the work, hut there was room for all. 'fhey had a capital at the last statement of accounts of £9.783,020 193 61. The great influence that Filen ily Snsietisis exerted inn country like ones, Was beyond conception. Every country was bett,r with having its citizens well care I for, comfortable arid happy. Their Society had that tendency to make men more comfortable and hapov. Tin made them bee- husbands and f others, and better members of society generally. The great influence that Friendly Societies had on this country wise the insulcation of thrift ; that alone was a crest cnnsileration. The savings , banks in this country.far oxclodsrl dvery other country, having regard to population, in its savings, and the," societies taught the young men to put away something ' for that time of sickness, so that he would be lade nen. I dent, and self-deleodent That was 'only one factor in connection with Friendly Soeie'ies, if it only did that it would he a grand work done in any country whatever country that might be. The re-oil was obedience to the law, every law. They ha 1 their ovn law, their bye-laws, district rules and general roles, and the very fact that they were tau:ht oloedienee to the rules of their society made them obedient to the laws of their country. The educational advantages of Friendly Societies was something worth talking about. He claimed that Friendly Societies planted in the b-east cal every man that spirit of self-dependence which be- came every man. On these four points alone, hp claimed that the Friendly Societies of this country had . been one of the greatest factors for gold in the history of our Country. It was understood and said by some unthinking brethren that they were paving too much into the society. The receints in 1897 for contributions were £892,837 13s 61.; for interest £310.988 41 111.; for entrance fees £3,419 Os 11d. The total re I ceipts were siok and funeral fund £1.207.024 19s 4d. They paid in 1897,if0r sick besefits £695,789 134 ad ; and they Paid for the funeral of wives and to widows £142 224 51 11. era total of £B3B 013 184 51. The con- tributions worked out at an average of £1 24 ni per imember, the average liability of each member paid for ' was £1 Is 41, so that last year they S sea paid le Avia over and above meeting their liabilities. The year before they had only paid 21 over; 3 year; ago they paid 61 less, so that they could quite see if they toolean average of 20 rears, they had paid 81 over and above meeting liabilities. That showed them that their tables of con- ' tribations and benefits were evenly balanced, and nobody was paving wore than their ordinary share. The tote! reecints under the different funds were £1 620.547 51 10d and the total payments £1.235,109 6s sd. The total gain on the year was £389.011 Os 73, the largest gain the M.U. had Ayer experienced. (Hear, fras); The admissions during 1897 were 49.632 ; deaths, 8,373 . seilessinns, 23,286. Now if every lodge in the Unity had ' a benevolent:fund in connection with it, these high per- centages of secessions would be very much reduced. sneaking of the South Wales coal strike he said the M.U. had sebseribed over £llOO 111 lv,ep the Welsh mAni- hmir in benefit. The net increase in numbers was 17,993. The adult male mernSem were 787.962, widews f r funeral benefits 10.950. juvenile members 110,906. honorary members 11.741. and lass but not least the Ifemale members, 72 lodges, 3,551 members, making the I total membership 925,110. He was glad to 8911 passed at the last A.M.C. that the fema'e members of their Drier were classed upon the same plane a^cl paid the same enntrib illons. and had the same benefits as m aie members. If the M.U. would go determinedly inte the matter of old ago pensMee there was scarcely a States- man in the country who would dare to say no. They must approach it carefully. He would give it to every man who hti tried all his life to keep himself from heM • a burden on the r ites. If a man went into the W orkho roe he lost Calliht, he ceased to he 3 eitizen They did not want, anything of that kind. They quitted their country to bell:the rifiliest in the world, and begs, and they wanted the In. habitants of that country to have something to keep them decently in their old age He believed that the greatest nortien of a man's leisure was spent in doing good. It was only by attßiStil.", one ano`h•r that they would do good in this world. If every man was a selfish individual and rally thought for himself, and those+ lin- meliatmly surrounding, what a world of misery they should have. Let them hone that the M.U. would go on in the van of Friendly Secieties. Make their lodges solvent, be determined to be solvent, and his earloi-e was, if there was any lodge in the district which would not el on the line, of reform, he should like to know which it was, and the Board would see they were put right. (Applause.) Song " Monareh of the Wonda." dr°. W. Devereux, gong, " The so'diers of the Queen " Bro. J. Anpleton

Bro.P.Connor in giving the toast of"Ashton-in-MakPr- field District," said they had 12,00 'members in the &s- -trict, to which that lodge contributed 480. There were five led Zes in the district; they had six, a couple of years age, but one became defunct. They had only £3OO and tha; was not enough to guarante3 the members 'he benefits they were promised on initiation, and so the ledge was broken up and made a tranch. He said if every man in the district would do his share there would be no such thing as insolvency. (Hear, hear.) Bro. George Wtight sang "Our Jack's come home to- day," Bro. McCormick gave "Billaraey," and Bro. B. Wright sang ."Trip it merrily."

80. G. Viiilson J.M.( should- hove responded to the previous toast but he was unavoidably absent. Bro. G. Crossley (Gar:tang lodge) gave tne toast of "The Viaduct lodge," and said it V 74.1 d surprise to hien to have to propose that toast,which was the toast of the evening. With regard to foreign members, be did not think the right hand of fellowship VMS held out to them as it ought to be. Through unfois.eu circumstances they were compelled to pay into the lodges where they' resided, as it did not pay to transfer. H 3 had spoken to several that night who did not even kno that the Anniversary was being held. Foreign members ought to know a little more about what was connected with, and what was going cio in tho lo ige. It Wi3 a question he felt very much upon. Bro. B. Connor said It was the fault of the foreign members. In that lodge they would allow a foreign member to take office and go through, but they would not let him vote, and it was not the fault of the lodge if the foreign members were ignorant of its affairs. (Hear hear.) Bro. John Hunt P.S., sang "Nil desperandum." Bro. Thane (secretary) responding to the lodge toast said he did not quite agree with the remarks of Bro. Crossley with regard to Foreign members,but he thought Bro. Connor had given him a complete answer. If the foreign members came up the lodge they would know as much as their own members. The income of the lodger sick and funeral fund was £638 23 id, thT chief itemS ware contributions £404, rent from invested money ia Property £172. Expenditure £BO4 103 91, sick par £39493 61, funerals £lB3 4s 8:1, rates and taxes £23 Is 4d. It spoke well for the stability of the lodge when it could meet an expenditure so large, and add to RS Capital a sum of £33, an amount which would be con- silerably increased. (Hear, hear ) The capital was £2517 91 4kd and they had 378 members, and they bad added this year over 30 members, mainly through the exertions of one or two of their members, PO that at the present time they had upwards of 400 naernbers oe the books. At their last anniversary Bro. Tunstall con- gratulated them for adopting tables for the admission of children into their lodge. He was sorry he coulsl not say that this had ben a great success, but ho hoped CO b able to tell him eo, if the members were on y true te the society. (Applause.) The other toasts were " Host and Hosts," propssei by Bro. W. Sut:on, " The lodge surgeon " proposed by Bro. John Jones, and" Visiting Brethren "proposed by Bro. F. Roberti, PG. In edition to those already menttoned,Bro. J. Clare sang several humorous songs. 'roe singing of the National Anthem brought the gathering to a close. ob.

TIM BURNING FATALITY AT WAnnitsoror.i. Mr. Jon's deputy-coroner held an inquiry on Saturday at the Police Parade-room, Warrington, into the cause ef the death of George Charles Clark, three years of age, who resided with his parents at 6, Keen-street. Mrs. Clark stated that at 10-30 en the previous Thursday morning she went to see her mother, who was ill, leaving her three children at breakfast. She was onIN away a few minutes, when her eldest child, NI ary (six years of age) came to tell her that her brother's clothes were on fire. The boy had been taken to the Infirmary before she returned to the house, and died at 7 p.m. the same night. A little daughter of the previous witness said her brother wee standing near the washing boiler show- ing his pinafore, which was in the water, to his younger brother, when his clothes ignited, and he was severely burnt about the face and body. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. MUNICIPAL ELECTION, NOVEMBER IST, 1898. TO THE ELECTORS CF THE TOWN HALL WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, Having been requested by a large number of the ratepayers of the ward to over myself as a candidate for the 1 vacancy at the ensuing Municipal Election, after due con- sideration, I have decided to do so. I Being a resident and ratepayer In the ward, I claim to know its wants, and if elected, its interests shall at all times have my best attention BOROUGH IMPROVEMENTS. I believe that by careful and good management, efficiency with economy can be obtained, and that the Rates of the Borough, which are now too high, can be reduced without interfering with necessary improvements, and also that it is desirable that some portion of Vie projected ctreet Improve- ments should be forthwith completed. INTRODUCTION OF' TRAMWAYS, The laying down of Tramways in the Borough is an urgent necessity. and. In my opinion, could be made in a short time a profitable source 0 revenue, a benefit to tradespeople, and a boon to the public. THE GAS QUESTION. The Council may not necessarily be weakened by the introduction of younger members, and the reduction in the price of gas which comes into operation on November Ist was undoubtedly brought about ky the energetic and persistent action of the young men in the Council. If elected, it shall be my earnest endeavour, not only to obtain an improvement in the quality, but also a further reduction in the price. My action upon the Council, if you do me the honour to elect me as your r.presentative shall be unbiassed by party considerations, and influenced only by a desire to be of some service to my fellow townsmen. I am, ladles and gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, JAMES HORTON. Crosileld-street, Warrington, October 14th, 1898.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. NOVEMBER, 1898. TO THE ELECTORS OF LATCHFORD WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, I beg to thank you for the honour conferred upon me in electing me as your representative in our Town Council for the past three years. During my term of office I have, to the best of lay ability, carried out your instructions. My devotion to your service will be observed by attention to the attested statement of attendances at Council and Committee Meetings for 1835.6, 1896-7, 1897-8. 1895-6. 1896-7. No. of No. of No. of No. of Atten. Meet. Atten. Meet. Council Meetings 13 13 Council Meetings 19 19 I School Attendance 18 20 School Attendance 19 20 I Museum, Ac 11 14 Museum. Ac 11 16 Town Hall, Ac 22 25 Town Hall, Ac 20 23 64 72 69 78 1897-8 up to and including 22nd September, 1898. No. of No. of Atten. Meet. Council Ma etings 14 14 School Attendance 18 18 Museum, /cc 10 12 Town Hall, do 21 21 -- 83 65 Total Meetings 215. Total Attendances 198. I save also promoted the formation and paving of our new streets and back passages, and the erection of additional gas lamps. The Council also adopted a motion proposed by myself that a recreation ground be provided for our Ward, which led up to the purchase of the Old Warps Estate. This has been dedicated to. and a portion set apart for the use of the people. and called Victoria Park. All these improve- ments will add to the health, happiness, and individual contentment of the people, which should be the object of all Local Clovernment. Much yet remains to be accomplished, and on the First of November you will be called upon to elect your representative for this important Ward. A large number of my friends have requested ms to allow myself to be nominated for re-election. which I have consen- ted to do. Should you again honour ITle with your confidence I shall, to the best of my ability, do all I can to promote the best interests of the elector.. It is a source of gratification to me to notice the progress which has been made in our Ward during the sixty years of my residence amongst you, and I confidently appeal to you for your vote and interest to again place me in the honourable position of your represen- tative, I beg ta remain, Ladles and Gentlemen, your obedient servant, LUKE ELLISON, 639, Knutsford-road, Latchford.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1898. TO TEIE BURGESSES OF FAIRFIELD WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— Three years ago you honoured me by electing me as your representative in the Town Council. Since that time I have andeavoured honestly and fearlessly to be faithful te the trust you then reposed in me. I have served upon the following important Committeesi viz. : Gas, Sanitary Works, Fire Engine, Markets, School Attendance, and Cemetery. In regard to the first three. named, I claim that my engineering and mechanical know- ledge and experience has been of substantial value to the whole of the Ratepayers. A great improvement has been effected in our Gas Works which will result in the immediate reduction of the price of gas. To this agreeable result I claim to have contributed. I am a member of the Sub-commitiee of the Sanitary Works at rongford, where we have had considerable success in the disposal of the town's refuse • but further imprGvements in this direction are Much needed, and are In course of accom- plishment. On all questions affecting Street Improvement, Paving, Lighting, and Sewerage I have endeavoured to do my best for you all. The important question of Dredging the River has occu- pied the attention of the Council for some time past, and it is absolutely necessary that the Rivers Committee should re- ceive the strong support of every member of the Corporation in their determination to prevent the Ship Canal Company from ignoring their just and legal resoonsibilities. The policy of the Rivers Committee has my warmest approval. I trust that the manner in which I have discharged my duties will justify you in extending to me a renewal of your confidence, as the experience which I have gained will certainly add to the value of my services to you in the future. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your Obedient Servant, DAVID S. DUNCAN. Padgate-lane, Warrington, October 17th, 1898.
